Numerical relativity simulations allow us to investigate the merger dynamics between equal-mass black holes surrounded by either wave dark matter or a massive stream of massive particles. In both scenarios, the gravitational interaction between the black holes and the dark matter generates significant forces that alter the merger evolution, leading to observable differences in the resulting gravitational waves compared to those from "naked" black holes. These structural discrepancies produce distinct signatures within multi-messenger astronomy: when an equal-mass black hole pair merges, the surrounding light dark matter fails to settle into a stable, emitting configuration, creating an imbalance between the radiation emitted gravitational fields and that of matter; conversely, for massive dark matter, the signal originates primarily from changes in the gravitational field that remain largely offset by changes in the material field and matter. Additionally, the final outcomes vary, with the event horizon often ejecting substantial amounts of the surrounding lighter matter while the concentrated core of heavy dark matter typically remains stable and emits signals after the event.

This research addresses the unresolved question of exponential stability for a specific Euler–Bernoulli beam model described on a metric graph with three uniform arms radiating in a star configuration. The outer vertices are simply supported (hinged), whereas the central node is elastically restrained against both translation and rotation. By analyzing the associated Sturm–Liouville-type differential equations, the paper confirms the existence of decoupled equations linked to either symmetric or antisymmetric eigenvectors. It further demonstrates that, regardless of the boundary parameter values, the antisymmetric mode cluster exhibits a constant separation between successive eigenvalues. Focusing particularly on the case where the central constraints are fully rigid (infinite stiffness), the analysis shows the approximation of these dynamics by a non-local, odd-symmetric PDE yields a Pritchard reduction: the system decomposes into an infinite-dimensional symmetric component and a fully characterized finite-dimensional interaction on the subspace spanned by the beam's odd eigenmodes. Together, these results enable the explicit construction of a global series-of-controls feedback law, ensuring exponential stability for the entire feedback closed-loop system.

A persistent conjecture posits that global symmetries cannot exist within quantum gravity. By examining extensive families of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, the possible generalized global symmetries and mechanisms to avoid them are investigated. Essential components in these theories are generalized $\theta$-terms, which establish non-linear couplings among axion fields and terms topological quadratic in gauge curvatures, thereby disrupting many global symmetries. Any resulting residual symmetries can also be broken if certain charged states exist. We produce Single-Photon Catalyzed Coherent States (SPCCSs) utilizing quantum optical methods, specifically through interaction between two modes where one carries a coherent wave and the other an individual photon. The analytical framework for these states accounts for various levels of detection efficiency. Our analysis explores their quantum behavior, highlighting non-classical features such as squeezed quadratures, sub-Poissonian statistics, and negative Wigner functions. Diverse strategies exist for tackling continuous-time dynamic optimization problems on computable trajectories, including collocation methods, shooting techniques, and dynamic programming. Conversely, artificial life and robotics subfields face significant constraints due to the high cost of these traditional approaches in real-time operation; consequently, these areas adopt simplified movement generation heuristics that, while suboptimal and not globally consistent, facilitate a rapid trade-off between performance and computational speed. Our research introduces "trapezoidal collocation," a decentralized, decentralized, and parameter-free procedure that transforms continuous-time dynamic optimization issues—lacking closed-form analytical solutions—into a set of independent problems tractable for a computer to resolve. Distinguishing itself through its decentralized architecture (where each agent solves a localized problem) and the absence of the need to store or adjust global trajectory parameters, our method still surpasses the limitations of current robotics and artificial life compromises by producing near-optimal paths within a decentralized framework. Consequently, our solution markedly extends these disciplines in terms of functional capability with only a marginal increase in computational time relative to them.

Delineating esophageal tumors in CT scans presents a dual challenge for manual and automatic segmentation: the low tissue contrast near the malignancy, the variable anatomy of the esophagus, and the occasional obscuring effect of foreign bodies like feeding tubes. Consequently, physicians often rely on supplementary data from endoscopy, electronic medical history, and alternative imaging modalities such as PET scans to inform segmentation tasks. Leveraging this auxiliary knowledge represents a vital strategy to enhance automatic CT-based detection systems. While prior research has focused primarily on diseases visible in direct contact with body cavities—utilizing methods to integrate clinical insights and endoscopic visuals for inferences on unmodified CT slices—the authors introduce a novel framework specifically tailored for endoluminal esophageal tumors. This approach integrates patient-specific endoscopic videos and structured EHR data to establish precise CT targets for automated analysis. The proposed method employs an end-to-end skimming protocol for initial endoscopy-driven estimate generation, augmented by structured risk stratification derived from EHR characteristics to refine CT segmentations via population-informed probability distributions. Evaluation utilizing the publicly accessible RISE dataset confirmed the method's robustness, with results extended to a secondary set of diverse cases for broader validation.

Offshore drilling incurs significant expenses, making well placement a critical factor in optimizing production and financial returns. "The well is steering," involves utilizing subsurface earth models, geological frameworks, and reservoir assessments to minimize uncertainty. Furthermore, integrating advanced imaging and data techniques enables visualisation beneath the ground surface, offering crucial insights for geologists and engineers to enhance decision-making in oil and gas exploration. These insights facilitate informed strategies to navigate wells more productively, ultimately leading to better operational outcomes in the sector.

Named entity recognition (NER) stands as a pivotal task in natural language processing and core technique for knowledge extraction, commonly employing structural variants of conditional random fields (CRF-structured techniques) to model target dependencies effectively. Nested named entity problems present a unique challenge where multiple entity levels coexist within specific documents. By utilizing a holistic modeling approach, this study aims to enhance current conditional approaches specifically for nested scenarios while preserving algorithmic efficiency. Through an innovative modification to the structural language approach, we introduce a new system designed for nested NER problems that ensures an optimal global solution exists. This system has been implemented, tested on public shared tasks, and found to be effective in successful knowledge extraction.

This study extends tropical methods to address the $\mathbb{A}^1$-enumeration of bitangents, analyzing tropical curves intersecting an extended extension-ordinary bitangent configuration. We define a specific class of pairs consisting of tropical bitangents and extension-ordinal whipple numbers. It is demonstrated that the number of such tropica l bitangent occurrences matches the number of valuations associated with complex bitangent hyperplanes, thereby establishing a key link between extended-ordinal ordinary tropic enumeration within $\mathbb{A}^1$ power series. This study also explores the multiplicity structure of tropical bitangents and demonstrates how this structure informs the stated enumeration process. This work is conditional upon the assumption of the Mandelbrot cycle.

Research into the localization of mobile nodes in wireless sensor networks remains highly active. This paper introduces a newly devised range-based positioning algorithm for ZigBee-enabled WSNs, utilizing RSSI signals, which accounts for path loss exponent effects, is simple to implement, and requires minimal computational resources. The study further analyzes the influence of the path loss exponent, demonstrating through testing that the algorithm achieves optimal accuracy with values between 2.5 and 3, supported by both practical experiments and theoretical frameworks. Accuracy is evaluated using practical data, which further substantiates the approach. The theoretical foundation supports this approach. Theoretical principles substantiate the methodology employed in this research. The study utilizes experimental results to validate its proposals. The theoretical context provides essential results for the validity of this work. The role of this algorithm under practical conditions is demonstrated through our results. The methodology presented ensures reliable operation based on our findings. The results confirm the effectiveness of this approach in practical scenarios.

Defined as advanced capability in two or more languages for both spoken and written communication, multilingualism frequently manifests through code-switching or code-mixing within individual sentences. This work reviews existing natural language processing (NLP) literature regarding its limitations and obstacles when addressing five critical social impact areas: crisis response, healthcare support, political engagement, anti-disinformation strategies, and hate speech mitigation in multilingual communities. Furthermore, we introduce prospective datasets, models, and utilities poised to propel multilingual NLP research toward broader societal benefits. Utilizing English-Hindi mixing as a case study allows for representative inferences applicable to other languages pairs.

Automatic image description models are typically built and assessed on crowd-sourced human references, with the top-performing system selected by measuring similarity against these references using metrics such as BLEU, CIDER, or METEOR. Consequently, since both system performance and evaluation accuracy hinge on these descriptions, it is crucial to ensure their high quality. However, similar to other natural language generation applications, a significant portion of the annotations in image captioning datasets contains low-quality examples. Therefore, this study aims to analyze the variability in captioning evaluation metrics and determines the threshold for filtering out descriptions that yield anomalous score readings. Our findings indicate that standard text similarity evaluations exhibit broad variability across different sub-samples of reference captions, with the extreme outliers—representing roughly 5% of the descriptions—causing this fluctuation. We recommend discuring scoring descriptions falling within the bottom 2 standard deviations to mitigate these effects. Furthermore, our results reveal that the proposed filtering method remains robust even when the evaluation dataset shifts to harder subsets containing fewer high-frequency images; conversable to this, the study evaluates descriptor reliability on two sub-segments of COCO 2014, showing that while score diversity slightly increases with harder subtitle sets, the proposed approach continues to identify problematic entries effectively.

Tantalum oxides (Ta$_2$O$_5$) exhibit favorable physical and chemical attributes, including strong proton ionization potential, prompting investigation into their potential use as radiosensitizers in hadrontherapy for cancer therapy. This study employs the X-ray photoelectron spectrometer (XPS) to analyze the electronic configuration of Ta$_2$O$_5$. Results from the Multi-Phy (MP) framework, which integrates ab initio multiple scattering methods with semi-empirical hybridization of scattering potentials, are compared against traditional experimental interpretations. The simulation successfully reproduces the experimental XPS data, with the best fit indicating that x-ray binding energies for Tetravalent and Hexavalent states are 5.22 eV and 5.82 eV, respectively, and a mix of oxidation states exists within the sample. Furthermore, the findings demonstrate the capacity of the MP code to exchange experimental data, aiding in understanding complex materials.

Previous research suggests that individual-level factors, such as personality traits, can influence the propagation of misinformation. However, a significant gap remains in understanding how such traits affect information circulation when examining large populations. This study investigates the relationship between a rigorous set of nationally representative data from four U.S. surveys (n = 14,800) and a prior national news tracking survey (n = 1,800) conducted shortly after a major piece of political false news. By analyzing these datasets, we demonstrate that before accounting for education levels, a person's standing on various news items is closely tied to their score on the Five-Factor Model (FFM) of personality. Notably, **conscientiousness** plays a specific role in this dynamic; individuals scoring higher are likely to encounter more news stories, including false information, simply due to elevated news consumption volumes rather than the specific algorithms of their news sources or their political allegiances. Consequently, highly conscientious people encounter political misinformation at higher rates compared to those who are neurotic, lazy, or open to experience, solely because of their habit of reading more content overall. Yet, this study also reveals a protective effect: among all news readers, those with strong conscientiousness actually encounter **less** misinformation than statistically predicted. We speculate that the organizational habits and self-discipline associated with high conscientiousness enable more effective news verification habits. Ultimately, these findings underscore the necessity of integrating personality data to fully comprehend misinformation dissemination

We propose integrating semi-supervised algorithms into suspicious event detection within data streams to enhance robustness against spam and improve resource efficiency. By leveraging existing labeled data alongside newly streamed labels, detection precision improves while costs remain low since streaming labeling is applied sparingly. Although numerous semi-supervised methods exist, most are unsuitable for erratic and rapid anomalies found in security contexts. Consequently, we developed a specialized streaming clustering method tailored for security data, utilizing streaming dimensionality reduction to enable effective labeling of novel data streams.

Human teachers often convey novel task skills through verbal and non-verbal cues, such as V-PLT, which encode information across spatial, temporal, and logical dimensions. Encoding these complex constraints into autonomous vehicle planning is non-trial. In this paper, we address the scenario in which various automotive skills generate constraints from audio recorded by instructors during on-site vehicle planning and control operations via a Sequential Plan Learning (V-PLT) approach. Specifically, we utilize spectral, pitch/chroma, and timbre characteristics to represent these data sets. We then propose a sequential loading algorithm for acquiring vehicle planning and control constraints from these feature streams, effectively enabling the structured acquisition of such data. Experiments using sound recordings from five vehicle planning and control strategies during test drives demonstrate that proposed method can accurately identify, isolate, extract, and integrate planning and control constraints from teacher-provided guidance.

Few-shot learning (FSL) is a significant research direction that aims to perform classification using very limited labeled data, typically relying on metric learning. A primary challenge in this area is adapting models trained on large datasets (source domains) to new tasks with scarce data (target domains), a process known as domain adaptation. Existing approaches to this often assume access to unlimited data from multiple related sources, an assumption that does not reflect reality. In contrast, this paper addresses the practical scenario of adapting to a single new domain requiring classification with only a small set of labeled samples. We introduce "Meta-Adaptation for One-To-One Domain Shift" (M3), a method designed to enhance real-world few-shot learning by updating domain-invariant features. Unlike previous techniques, our framework does not need to learn from unlimited data from one or more sources; instead, it acquires and adapts features from the specific new task itself during the training phase using one-to-one domain setup assumptions. Experiments across several standard benchmarks confirm that our method surpasses state-of-the-art results in the setting of adapting to a single new domain with few samples, demonstrating significant improvements in practical applicability.

Cross-domain recommendation (CDR) has gained significant traction due to its ability to enhance user experiences, yet the majority of existing approaches suffer from distribution shifts that hinder performance. Furthermore, the development of multiple compatible CDR sources is rarely addressed. To address these issues, we introduce the Multi-Sparse-Domain Collaborative Relation (MSCR) model. This model not only addresses the dispute in capacity-building recommendation (CR) literature but also accounts for the scarcity encountered in various other recommendation domains. By incorporating a domain-adapter (DA) structure, the proposed model mitigates performance degradation, ensuring that both sparse- and dense-populated recommendations maintain high quality within the unified framework. Additionally, the model enables users to access diverse goods by integrating multi-sparsity and domain-adaptive (MSDA) components, which have been designed to incorporate implicit user preferences into the learning objectives function. Extensive experiments conducted on eight datasets demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed model, which has been validated against nine other datasets.

Numerous convex optimization tasks involve minimizing a differentiable objective subject to nonnegativity constraints on variables belonging to a cone defined by the equality constraints of an orthogonal direct sum decomposition. When this dividing cone matches the geometric structure described in prior research, well-developed algorithms and duality techniques are available. Conversely, if the cone does not match this structure, researchers have previously defined "exotic cones" and established dualities specifically to handle such cases. This work aims to broaden the class of feasible problems allowable by these methodologies. We achieve this by introducing a broader category of cones—formally termed $\mathcal{F}$-cones—for which the associated optimization frameworks and their duals remain valid. The authors further demonstrate an algorithm to determine the corresponding dual cone for $\mathcal{F}$-cones and derive a formula that ties these dual $\mathcal{F}$-cones to the geometric multiplex of the problem. At a core level, our main contribution is the utilization of a specific family of piecewise-linear, convex functions known as angle maps, which are shown to be intimately connected with the duality relationship between a given $\mathcal{F}$-cone and its dual.

Rapidly maturing automated quality control (QC) systems are vital for ensuring MRI analytics produce dependable outcomes, which is only possible through consistently well-standardized inputs and robust processing. These systems must account for significant inter-scanner variability to ensure reliability. Although such programs require extensive future validation, they do necessitate standardized metadata to guarantee input consistency. This study evaluates whether current QC algorithms demonstrate generalizability across sites and vendors by analyzing how metadata influences their performance. Using data from the Multi-Modal MRI Data Contribution, we conducted parallel QC processing on 1,080 pre-scan-categorized, multi-center, and multi-manufacturer scans from the Multi-Modal MRI Project using OpenData. We compared key output metrics against established per-scan rejection criteria to determine if performance metrics—such as inter-scan similarity or intra-scan consistency—varied significantly due to site, scanner, or specific metadata. Our findings indicate that while some metadata categories notably impact QC performance, the effects are minimal for the majority of measures and reach statistical significance only when sample volumes are large enough. These results support the conclusion that modern automated QC methods are becoming sufficiently robust for real-world deployment.

This paper examines the impact of privately owned electric vehicles on power system stability during disruptions. To capture the decentralized interactions within transportation and energy domains, we introduce a Network-based Multi-Agent Optimization with Equilibrium Constraints (N-MOPEC) framework. Specifically designed for a high-dimensional non-convex problem, our solution employs a specialized algorithm relying on precise convex reformulation. Extensive numerical experiments validate both the proposed methodology's efficacy in visualization and its potential policy ramifications, establishing a robust basis to advance resilience research on integrated transportation-power networks influenced by private EVs.

The release of the Intel Optane DC Persistent Memory Module (Optane DC PMM) has finally made scalable non-volatile memory accessible on general-purpose processors. This technology offers significantly lower cost per byte compared to DRAM while maintaining comparable speeds, bridging the performance and economic gaps between main memory and large disk-backed storage. Achieving this requires a three-way hierarchy: general-purpose applications must automatically and transparently utilize DRAM for speed-critical operations, employ Optane DC PMM as high-capacity main memory, and leverage virtualization techniques to hide the discrepancies between the implemented memory system and application expectations. To realize these architectural goals, precise modeling is essential; however, existing simulations of non-volatile memory systems are too weak to accurately capture the intricate interactions among software applications, the scheduling algorithms of memory consistency models, and hardware behaviors. To address this deficiency, this paper introduces "Persistent Memory Simulator" (PerSim), a versatile and modular framework designed specifically to simulate consistent memory systems. By integrating flexible co-schedulers and simulating multiple architectures simultaneously, users can deploy various applications to stress-test persistent memory systems efficiently. Empirical results demonstrate that using PerSim enables researchers to conduct robust evaluation environments capable of accurately reflecting complex, cutting-edge non-volatile memory scenarios.

Recent work proposed the Motivation Dynamics framework, which applies bifurcations to model autonomous mobile decision-making. This current research extends that approach to address systems with multiple agents by demonstrating its adaptability for encoding durable rendezvous patterns. Through analytical characterisation of bifurction properties and numerical analysis, we illustrate how the framework successfully captures the emergence of complex, data-driven phenomena.

Magnetization data for the alloys as a function of field strength and concentration align closely with experimental observations. Furthermore, the anomalous Seebeck coefficient peak associated with the Curie temperature in the Gd$_x$Cm$_{1-x}$Sn$_3$ alloys offers additional support for their AFM-to-FM transition. Resistivity measurements for the alloys exhibit a sawtooth pattern

Developing robust, high-performance interfaces between silicon telecom photons and spins will significantly advance global quantum networks. T radiation damage centres in silicon are a promising candidate for such interfaces, offering long lifetimes for both nuclear and electron spins alongside an optically distinct, narrow O-band transition centered near 1326 nm. Furthermore, we establish a methodology leveraging spin-selective optical transitions to assess intrinsic spectral diffusi'on characteristics in these T center collections. Medical Resonance Imaging, or MRI, utilizes radio waves for scanning the human body as part of tomographic imaging within the radiology spectrum. As a painless and efficient diagnostic method, MRI facilitates the creation of clear anatomical images and the observation of physiological activities within the torso, enabling medical experts to begin detecting and treating ailments immediately. While these are standard features, an essential but often overlooked capability is its exceptional data filtering ability. When combined, even a small collection of MRI angles yields sufficient data for effective image reconstruction through the use of Compressed Sensing, or CS. However, implementing CS requires an underlying "prior," commonly interpreted as assuming image sparsity across certain transforms. This study moves away that constraint by introducing a learning-free approach to a novel prior that requires no image data. This methodology presents the implementation of a sparse transform via the representation of isotropic 3D cubic B-spline networks. Finally, this sparse transformation enables the application of CS in the reconstruction of MRI volumes.

Recent advancements in machine learning have created a demand for models capable of learning from non-independent data sources. A significant challenge remains in extending effective regularization techniques to handle long-memory processes within high-dimensional frameworks where the number of parameters exceeds the sample size. This paper investigates estimation performance in high-dimensional linear regression models under long-range dependence. Specifically, we demonstrate that for the sample size $n$ and parameter count $p$, the risk bounds closely resemble those derived from independent data, merely incurring a specific cost related to the sample's dependence structure. Moreover, we introduce a novel data preprocessing strategy that relaxes the requirements on the stationary process, altering only the concept of independence to a mixing condition with temporal blocks, while preserving risk performance analogous to independent observations in terms of $n$, $p$, and memory parameters. Final results confirm that our approach achieves the optimal risk metric, broadly defined by $n$, $p$, and memory parameters, under rather straightforward assumptions.

Speech enhancement serves as a vital pillar for other significant audio technologies, including speech recognition and synthesis, holding major importance in the field. This study presents a new deep learning framework for this task, which implements a comprehensive attention mechanism integrated with a bidirectional sequence-to-sequence approach to exploit all available latent details following key sampling frames. Expanding upon existing attention-driven recurrent networks, this proposed bidirectional attentional design achieves an improved performance quality regarding the PESQ score, surpassing results from baselines OM-LSA, CNN-LSTM, T-GSA, as well as its unidirectional attentional LSTM counterpart.

Bio-Safety Levels (BSLs) define containment standards for infectious agents in laboratories globally, with Negative Pressure Rooms (NPRs) being critical infrastructure at BSL-3 and BSL-4 levels. By maintaining internal pressure lower than the exterior, NPRs force airborne pathogens to flow outward, preventing entry. However, the definitive utility of these facilities—such as the safety duration for personnel inside after containment failure—and the optimal effectiveness of Negative Pressure Systems (NPS) remain poorly understood due to challenges in direct internal pressure monitoring. Consequently, this study utilizes an experimental setup to examine stable negative pressure conditions in both an isolated chamber and one connected to an airlock, employing the acoustic speed of sound to calculate the negative gauge pressure within the NPR via acoustic travel time (AT) measurements taken at multiple points. Results allow gauge pressure in the test volume to be derived directly from AT data using a dedicated model and validated by physical barometric readings, demonstrating a linear relationship with the square root of the inverted squared AT. Furthermore, incorporating these AT results into existing mass balance equations enabled the estimation of air infiltration rates, yielding values of $0.1$ m³/hour for the single chamber and $0.36$ m³/hour for the chamber-plus-airlock configuration. Ultimately, the work addresses two key gaps: estimating the internal exposure time for personnel and determining the effective number of Air Changes Per Hour (ACH) for stabilization, offering a novel, AT-based method to assess NPR

Storage is vital for providing firm power in decarbonized electric systems. However, retrospective analyses often reveal that storage providers may neglect acting on robust pricing signals during periods of scarcity. Although this phenomenon has traditionally been blamed on forecasting mistakes or operational breakdowns, this paper argues instead that it stems from the strategies employed in risk-averse unit scheduling. By implementing a stochastic self-dispatch model utilizing actual data from Australia’s National Electricity Market, the authors show that storage entities driven by fear of risk tend to sell excessive capacity immediately when prices rise and delay purchases until volatility subsides following peak rates. Consequently, this risk-influenced scheduling behavior explains why these resources illuminate lights early in upward price spikes and power them later in downward trends, a pattern that mirrors the unreliable performance observed in historical records.

Within quantum systems, the evolution of superposition states between electronic configurations occurs on ultrafast scales (ranging from attoseconds to femtoseconds, where one attosecond equals 10$^{-18}$ seconds), resulting in charge densities that vary with time. By utilizing the inaugural attosecond-precision soft x-ray pulses generated by an x-ray free-electron laser, this study induces a coherent core-hole excitation within nitric oxide molecules. Furthermore, a circularly polarized infrared laser pulse serves as a timing reference ("attoclock"), rendering electron dynamics visible and allowing control over coherent electron motion by adjusting the photon energy of the incident x-ray pulse. Moreover, core-excited states constitute an ideal experimental platform for probing coherent electron behavior within matter that is highly energetic and exhibits strong correlations.

We investigated an Earth-atmosphere general circulation model within rotating, differentially rotating, and stratified spherical geometry, focusing on how various rotation rates generate multiple zonal jets at low viscosity. In the specific context of Earth's rotation rate, atmospheric jet structures align closely with predictions made by simplified partial models, including those accounting for stratification and rotation alone. Deviations between the full atmospheric model and simplified reduced models are primarily seen in meridional variations in jet amplitude rather than in overall pattern structures. Additionally, we examined the influence of transient waves and found that while they contribute to angular momentum transport on their own, they are unnecessary for the emergence of high-rotation multi-jet configurations displayed in both simple and complete atmospheric models.

Active learning (AL) seeks to identify an optimal subset of data for labeling that maximizes model performance, minimizing costs associated with the annotation process. Although deep neural networks have gained widespread adoption in various data-centric settings, the critical combination of active learning with deep architecture remains problematic, particularly when high labeling costs necessitate careful selection. To address this, we propose a novel methodology that integrates active learning strategies with self-supervised pretraining. In the initial phase, a large dataset undergoes pretraining using self-supervised techniques, during which unlabeled data subsamples are actively chosen. In the subsequent stage, this selected data subset is used for final labeling and fine-tuning. It is important to note that the initial phase capitalizes on data utility following extensive pretraining, whereas the final phase operates after extensive prior exposure, during which samples are most valuable for reducing costs. We illustrate the practical application of this two-phase framework on the Supervised Contrastive Learning (SupCon) model, demonstrating its success when used with subsets of the Caltech-OCR (COCR) dataset. Results demonstrate that this proposed method achieves superior accuracy relative to standard active learning approaches applied to SupCon, without incurring additional labeling expenses.

This paper explores fresh analytical and geometric aspects of generalized algebraic multiplicity (χ), which originated in works [7, 5] and was subsequently advanced via [20, 23, 24]. Notably, it uncovers a brand-new relationship between χ and the local intersection index of algebraic varieties—a cornerstone of Algebraic Geometry—thereby granting χ significant geometric significance within the framework of Nonlinear Spectral Theory. Furthermore, a characterization of χ emerges from introducing a new concept: the local determinant of the Schur operator linked to the associated linear path, $\mathfrak{L}(\lambda)$, effectively tying Nonlinear Spectral Theory closer with those in Algebraic and Complex Analysis.

We introduce a proposal to simulate bosonic pair production by utilizing large ensembles of long-lived multilevel dipole particles coupled to a sub-dynamically driven optical resonator. Entanglement among these atoms, arising from the swapping of virtual photons via a shared optical cavity, increases exponentially over time. To overcome this challenge, we introduce slow-variation of one parameter of an ensemble-based mapping of dipoles to dipoles. This strategy moves us towards manageable multi-party quantum states and allows us to estimate an idealized effective interaction. Numerical simulations indicate this approach can effectively characterize Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) associated with multiple quantum states. This simulation advances our grasp of multipartite quantum correlation estimation and informs strategies for more efficient QFI evaluation in larger systems.

Donor spins in silicon have already reached benchmark record-breaking coherence times and single-qubit gate fidelities. The subsequent phase of development centers on demonstrating robust two-qubit logic operations, for which the exchange interaction serves as the most favorable coupling mechanism. To facilitate the efficient design of scalable donar-based quantum computers, we simulated the two-electron wave function using full configuration interaction methods integrated with multi-valley effective mass theory. Leveraging our code's high computational efficiency, we examined the exchange interaction, valley occupation probabilities, and electron spatial distributions for pairs of phosphorus donors across diverse lattice positions, orientations, and varying electric field strengths. These results are presented through interactive visualizations that dynamically trace valley and orbital components as donor sites change. Ultimately, our study offers a physically clear and quantitatively precise pathway for placing two-qubits optimally to maximize coupling exchange interaction and engineer valley suppression through external or intrinsic electric fields.

We analyze the transport characteristics of HgTe quantum wells with critical thickness, a regime where the band gap closes and the low-energy spectrum is described by a two‑dimensional Dirac Hamiltonian. Under applied pressure, this setup exhibits both longitudinal and diagonal Hall resistivity patterns. Using a simplified model where only localized states near the Dirac point are considered, we demonstrate that a Landau level forms precisely at zero energy within the converted bulk bands. This level supports spin‑dependent, fingers-like edge states (reminiscent of the quantum Hall effect in an inhomogeneous magnetic Landau lattice pattern generated by the quantum well structures). The formation and arrangement of these spin-split Landau levels and their corresponding edge modes accurately predict the observed quantum anomalous Hall effect effects, particularly explaining how the $\sigma_{xx}$ resistance peak sharpens and moves upward as the magnetic field increases. Additionally, we note discrepancies between model calculations and experimental data regarding resistance valley depths, hypothesizing these variations arise from non-resonant contributions originating outside the Dirac points. Overall, our results support the conclusion that the quantum anomalous Hall effect in HgTe quantum wells originates largely from localized states confined to the Dirac region of the inverted bulk bands.

Vehicular Communication (VC) protocols significantly contribute to accident avoidance by facilitating warning transmissions, a benefit that is particularly critical at road intersections due to elevated risks of collisions there. Concurrently, Non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA) stands as a robust solution for fifth-generation (5G) wireless networks. This paper introduces and analyzes the Adaptive Cooperative NOMA (ACN) protocol tailored for vehicular safety messages delivered from one source to two destinations, accounting for interference from other road vehicles whose locations follow a Poison Point Process. Closed-form mathematical expressions were derived to quantify both transmission outage probabilities. Furthermore, a comparison with existing methods demonstrates that the ACN protocol achieves notably lower out-ofage probabilities, especially within congested intersection environments, while also enhancing overall performance with increased user rates.

Dynamic time-division duplexing (TDD) allows each base station to schedule uplink and downlink transmission modes independently according to its own traffic load. Unfortunately, this decentralization leads to intercell cross-interference, making the combined problem of power distribution and resource allocation a mixed-integer non-convex challenge that is NP-hard. To address this, we introduce a computationally efficient, decentralized framework that decouples the scheduling and power control processes. The proposed method first distributes power across cells in a decentralized manner and subsequently assigns transmission modes using a non-cooperative game to reach a mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium. Two different payoff calculation methods within the game model explore the impact of cross-interference representations and the associated communication overhead. Simulation studies in an outdoor, high-density small-scale cellular environment demonstrate that these proposed strategies significantly surpass the performance of static TDD systems.

Despite numerous theories, the origin of the Hall anomaly observed in the mixed-state Hall resistivity of type-II superconductors remains unconfirmed by the scientific community. In this study, we performed a quantitative evaluation of magnetotransport data from Zn-doped V$_2$O$_3$, demonstrating that the anomaly arises from vacancy dynamics within a vortex lattice supported by a pinned vortex glass phase involving vortices, antivortices, vacancies, and inter-vortex charge carriers. This model accurately predicts the temperature-dependent peak in the anomalous portion of longitudinal resistivity seen in prior research. Furthermore, our findings suggest this phenomenon originates from vortex dynamics specifically tied to $1/3$-fluxon vortices composed of vortices, vacancies, and antivortices, distinguishing itself from existing alternatives which implicate volume-averaging methods, velocity vector discontinuities, or vacuum fluctuations. This result offers a reliable theoretical framework for future investigations into the underlying cause of the Hall anomaly in vortex systems.

Specifically, a continuous critical surface emerges instead when the correlation length diverges continuously through multiple directions. This study further examines how the phase transition dynamics change across different models, particularly comparing the 2D Ising with the 3D Landau framework where only a single critical point exists due to the distinct divergence pattern of the correlation along one direction only, reinforcing fixed-point behavior at specific values in the 3D Landau case only. Additionally it highlights implications regarding the CP search strategy applied experimentally given these differing theoretical signatures.

Detecting prohibited objects in x-ray imaging is vital for public safety, a task frequently challenged by objects with uniform coloration and poor texture, often leading to subpar results. To address the paucity of dedicated datasets necessitating few recent studies, this research introduces HiXray, the largest high-quality database for security inspections comprising 102,923 real-world prohibited items across eight categories and meticulously annotated by expert security personnel. Furthermore, to enhance detection accuracy regarding overlapping objects and irrelevant details, we propose a Lateral Inhibition Module (LIM). Inspired by how human vision suppresses noise to focus salient features, LIM functions through two specialized mechanisms: the Bidirectional Propagation (BP) unit drastically reduces noise interference from multiple sources, while the Boundary Suppression (BS) unit minimizes focus on background distractions. Additionally, boundary suppression helps mitigate the common "centering bias," where models incorrectly predict rectangular enclosures tightly but poorly aligned at object edges. Our comprehensive evaluations confirm that utilizing both components in LIM yields a Comprehensive Accuracy (mAP) improvement of +2.8% on the new HiXray benchmark, surpassing over 50 state-of-the-art models, with significant gains specifically observed in multi-class overlap scenarios and category-specific performance.

This paper investigates the deployment of differential privacy (DP) within graph-structured environments. It examines various DP formulations applicable both to publishing data and associated statistics, and to conducting machine learning on graph-based information, specifically focusing on graph neural networks (GNNs). Recognizing these intricate issues and the divergent interpretations of DP in graphs, we systematically organize existing literature into four key subfields. Finally, we highlight prominent open questions and promising avenues for future research.

Hydrodynamic theories provide effective strategies for simulating the dynamics of quantum many-body systems, which are otherwise computationally expensive. In this paper, utilizing the positive-P phase-space framework, we develop an novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for interacting Bose gases. Unlike current methods like generalized or superfluid hydrodynamics, this framework captures complete quantum dynamics, including non-equilibrium correlations and short-wavelength behaviors. We establish a linearized version of these positive-P equations to analyze correlation functions over both short and long time scales, confirming their excellent agreement with exact quantum results regardless of system size. Furthermore, we demonstrate its capability to model interacting Bose gases under various potentials, such as traps and lattice structures, as well as out-of-equilibrium scenarios like quantum quenching and real-time processes involving black hole formation in analog gravity contexts.

Temporal action detection focuses on identifying the start and end points of actions within a video. While current methods rely on dividing videos into non-overlapping segments for classification, this segmentation strategy introduces significant errors at boundary regions that can degrade performance. To address this, we introduce a new loss function based on binary segmentation adapted for temporal action detection. Our approach reframe the task by segmenting the duration of each video into labels corresponding to action segments and non-action background, aiming to directly and accurately locate action boundaries. Our methodology introduces an innovative shift in modeling video-level temporal events as precise segmentation problems, differing fundamentally from the standard classification of interval start and stop points. We evaluate our technique on two public benchmarks, MRVD and TVQA; the results demonstrate that our approach significantly improves boundary precision, especially when compared to conventional loss functions, establishing our method as state-of-the-art for temporal action detection.

Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS) technology has recently gained prominence as a cost-effective solution for enhancing wireless systems by managing the radio environment. This paper focuses on integrating an IRS into radar systems to enhance overall performance, with a specific examination of active antenna systems coupled with an ideal, element-specific, and controllable metasurface. Analyzing the characteristics of these bidirectional, multi-bounced, and reciprocal signals offers insights into target parameter accuracy—factoring in both direct and reflected path time delays—as well as potential location ambiguities arising from the return signal analysis. Simulation outcomes confirm these findings, highlighting that estimating parameters based on the multi-bounced signal alone yields lower accuracy compared to utilizing combined multi-bounced and direct signals for optimization.

**Objective:** This study aims to develop and evaluate a free-breathing T2-weighted turbo spin echo (TSE) sequence in 4D (3D plus respiration) tailored for respiratory motion compensation in the phase encoding direction.

**Approach:** The proposed 4TSE technique integrates a segmented 3D T2-weighted turbo spin echo sequence with a single-shot real-time 3D T2-weighted turbo spin echo sequence. This design ensures that the duration of the radio frequency (RF) pulse cycle remains constant, regardless of the amount of motion-compensated encoding steps required at any moment during breathing.

**Validation:** Feasibility verification involved healthy adult volunteers, while image quality assessments utilized phantom data, clinical scans, and compared key metrics against our previously published retrospective motion correction method.

**Findings:** The results demonstrate minimal through-plane motion artifacts, with a ratio of signal intensity to averaged signal intensity (SIR) of 17.5 ± 14% observed in liver imaging. Furthermore, no statistically significant image quality differences were detected when comparing the acquired 4D data to that obtained via the retrospective correction approach.

**Conclusion:** The new technique offers the practical advantages of a single breath-hold acquisition combined with the high image fidelity needed for robust 4D volumetric assessment.

Inter-orbital coupling denotes the capability to stimulate one atomic or molecular excitation state relative to another from an identical initial state, a feature typically restricted to a precise set of initial states known as coupling resonances. Drawing inspiration from wavelength coupling in photonic lattices, we demonstrate that inter-orbital coupling can be successfully achieved near-band-edge conditions close to the Rayleigh limit, enabling near-resonant photogeneration across multiple target states rather than just one. Consequently, this strategy facilitates the creation of robust cross-phases between different states—functioning as an atomic version of optical coupling—ideal for information readout in photonic qubits and quantum networks involving atomic nodes.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves the enhancement of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) in materials positioned near an interface with a high-SOC constituent, generating phenomena attributable to both intrinsic and spin-scattering-induced SOC. This review examines theoretical frameworks and experimental techniques for identifying and distinguishing between intrinsic proximity SOC and induced states through spin scattering within the interface and bulk of the weak-link material itself. Methods such as spin-resolved photoemission spectroscopy, angle-resolved spin-orbit Kerr effect spectroscopy, and angle-resolved spin-ARPES are highlighted for their capability to probe spin textures across adjacent layers individually and separately. Furthermore, the unique role of time-domain terahertz spectroscopy is emphasized; by capturing spin precession dynamics during Kerr rotation in thin-film stacks, it can resolve spin orientations with sufficient resolution to distinguish proximity-induced states from bulk characteristics.

This study explores imposing explicit Lipschitz constraints on neural network architectures to ensure stability with respect to inputs. We introduce a method for calculating an upper bound of the Lipschitz constant across various $p$-norms for typical feedforward layers and use it to frame neural network training with bounded dynamics as a constrained optimization task soluble via projected stochastic gradients. Results reveal these models outperform those trained using standard regularizers. Furthermore, we show that the hyperparameters require only intuitive adjustment and do not involve a complex trade-off, as is often necessary when applying regularization techniques. Comparative analyses with state-of-the-art models demonstrate enhanced robustness against adversarial disturbances and noisy data.

Sequential neural network models are valuable assets across numerous Natural Language Processing applications, yet their linear architecture frequently results in suboptimal benchmarks. This decline is particularly evident in Basque resource-rich tasks such as predicting morphological agreement, where English counterparts using the same networks perform significantly worse. In this study, we introduce Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) as an innovative architecture for this specific task, utilizing the high-valued CTSB morphological bank to convert each word in a sentence into a CTSB entry and processing sequences of words via their respective sequence-of-graph representations. Ultimately, our method learns to traverse these linguistic graphs to identify agreement features, achieving a state-of-the-art benchmark of 84.8% F1 on the testing set for the Basque agreement task.

Specifically, precessional effects can alter total received radiation by up to 1000% and surface heating variability by 200% and more across different regions, including those potentially in the gold zone or further inland areas as well as those slightly shifted toward cooler zones or smaller planets within our own solar system where this level of fluctuation wouldn't occur simultaneously with other major fluctuations like those seen here on Earth today but perhaps without accompanying fluctuations like tidal forces acting together here. While modified digital games effectively foster motivation for repetitive motor rehabilitation exercises, crafting alterations that successfully meet both therapeutic and engaging objectives remains difficult. We introduce an approach utilizing a statistical model of baseline player behavior to facilitate the successful integration of rehabilitation-specific objectives into the game modification process. By employing factor analysis to examine behavior data from unmodified gameplay during the design phase, we achieve dimensionality reduction to create player profiles. Using inference methods during the modification phase within observed players on updated versions allows us to evaluate potential shifts in behavior relative to these established profiles under various success metrics for different user demographics and practice stages. Experiments using an ex-co player game model during practice sessions for individuals undergoing rehabilitation from upper-limb extension following injury demonstrate the application of our technique using both qualitative and quantitative benchmarks using both quantification models (support vector regression) and human assessors. Results indicate that our approach can utilize both quantitative and qualitative metrics in utilizing only models to identify modifications that incorporate rehabilitation goals without negatively impacting overall user engagement.

To address recent indications of lepton-flavour non-universality observed in $b \to c \ell \nu$ and $b \to s \ell^+ \ell^-$ transitions, this investigation examines Drell-Yan dipositron pairs at CERN's LHC via third-generation gauge vector leptoquarks. Leveraging full kinematic distributions within an effective field framework, we evaluate the potential of NNLO QCD corrections derived from a chromomagnetic vector leptoquark operator. We contrast our results with a recent calculation based on the diphotron contact interaction; conversely to that approach, our model ensures full gauge invariance and incorporates NNLO precision. Additionally, we present exclusion regions for the leptoquark parameters under non-universal ($g_{t_e^c E^c L} \neq g_{t_e^ c \bar{E} L}$) and universal ($g_{t_e^ c \bar{E} L}$) couplings regarding the lepton chiralities. We further explore the impact of forthcoming dataset from Run 3 and the High-Luminosity LHC phases.

Radiation constraints inherent to positron emission tomography (PET) imaging hinder its application for studying vulnerable groups such as pregnant women, children, and animals, thereby restricting scientific advancement. This challenge stems from the standard reliance on radiotracers manufactured at cyclone facilities, which utilize neutron activation to convert stable target nuclei into radioactive isotopes, inevitably yielding radiopharmaceuticals contaminated with long-lived radiocarbon ($^{14}\text{C}$). Because $^{14}\text{C}$ has an extensive half-life of approximately 8,000 years, even trace amounts of this contaminant mask the low-count-rate data necessary for safe PET scans on sensitive populations. However, considering that many emerging radiotracers operate on recently developed imaging modes highly resistant to random coincidence noise—even from minimal background signals—we investigate the feasibility of purifying radiochemical batches to eliminate $^{14}\text{C}$ impurities. Furthermore, we assess the potential of producing radiotracers in the form of "total purity" solutions containing no other radiocarbons, thereby enabling safe and effective PET visualization for animals, children, and expectant mothers.

The challenges of news curation and personalization remain unsolved. Increasingly, individuals are worried about their data being excessively collected and used for questionable purposes disguised as customization. Insightful strategies by our team to create publisher-focused tools that prioritize privacy prompted a closer look at user concerns. Through survey research analyzing responses across various age demographics, this paper highlights critical findings to guide both editors and developers on refining the next wave of algorithm-driven recommendation engines, ensuring they successfully balance user experience with privacy by centering human interests.

Centering Theory (Grosz et al., 1995) analyzes how the structural components of conversation maintain local coherence through successive utterances referencing shared entities. This study explores the relationship between Centering Theory and current coreference resolution systems. We systematically assess whether neural coreference solvers align with Centering Theory rules by operationalizing the theory, constructing discourse-specific metrics, and employing a search-based framework. Results from an information-theoretic approach indicate a positive correlation between centering concepts and coreference; however, they suggest high-performing neural resolvers derive limited additional advantage from explicitly integrating these ideas. Furthermore, our findings demonstrate that pretrained context-aware embeddings inherently encode much of this coherence information, which likely explains why Centering Theory does not significantly boost their performance further.

WiFi fingerprints, which utilize collected Received Signal Strength Indicator (RSSI) references for known locations, have emerged as a widely adopted method for indoor positioning. These fingerprints serve as a critical component of my research, facilitating the precise mapping and analysis of signal strength patterns. Building upon this approach, the study introduces the concept of a "super-fingerprint," representing the aggregate of all available fingerprints. This innovative framework enables the demonstration and utilization of "super-location tracking," a continuous stream of positional data synthesized from the entire dataset. Furthermore, a novel statistical technique for locating anomalies in spatial environments is presented; this method operates directly on super-fingerprints and has been empirically demonstrated to remain robust and effective even amidst substantial noise and variability inherent in WiFi signals.

For over a century, the Fermi Paradox has puzzled scientists by asking why, despite Earth's vast history as a habitable planet, we have detected no signs of advanced space-faring civilizations. In his 1960 paper "Extra-Terrestrial Intelligence," Dyson proposed that one solution to this mystery is the existence of a "Dyson Sphere," a megastructure capable of harnnssing a star's total energy. Currently under development, this idea remains within theoretical reach. Because our own Sun is warm and bright, it could theoretically support life even within such a sphere; thus, these entities would likely appear as multi-planetary systems orbiting their host star. While we have yet to discover any that match our planet's level of advancement, ongoing searches at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) and the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope (JWWS) offer promising avenues for their detection.

Critical networked services are a primary revenue source for operators but are governed by Service Level Agreements (SLAs), necessitating rigorous service level monitoring. A prevalent approach utilizes active measurement probes that inject synthetic traffic to calculate performance metrics; however, this method is resource-intensive and limited in coverage, often causing undetected SLA breaches. Furthermore, human administrators typically define these limited monitoring zones, resulting in scalability issues and an inability to cope with highly dynamic networking patterns. This paper investigates the advantages of Peer-to-Peer (P2P) technology in enhancing SLA violation detection. It begins by outlining decentralized decision-making principles for steering active measurements via a self-organizing overlay. Secondly, it introduces activation strategies that leverage this approach, comprising both manual and fully autonomous solutions that empower individual peers to initiate monitoring sessions. Finally, the authors present the first implementation of these SLA detection mechanisms using the JXTA P2P framework, while evaluating performance through comparative analysis.

Beam breakup instability constitutes a critical challenge across particle accelerators, often determining both the maximum beam current and energy attainable. In linear accelerators (linacs), this phenomenon arises primarily from feedback caused by particles interacting with structures that have both the bunch and return paths interacting with structure that possess memory (capacitance). To address this issue, the research presented utilizes the theoretical models proposed by B. S. Guo and E. G. B. S. to simulate buncher systems. The study explores how varying specific parameters, including capacitance values and tuning the bunching element, can mitigate beam breakup instability and offer improvements in both system robustness and overall performance.

Precise long‑baseline neutrino oscillation experiments aim to determine oscillation parameters by depending heavily on accurate neutrino-nucleus interaction models, a source of significant systematic uncertainty largely because existing detectors struggle to distinguish nuclear species effectively. To address this limitation, three‑dimensional (3D) projection scintillator trackers have been introduced; these devices utilize fast-timing readout and external cathode‑ode (CSDP) readout of scintillator plates to provide detailed event event reconstruction in all three spatial dimensions. By clearly resolving nuclear de‑excitation gammas from nuclear recoil events, these trackers enable the identification of target nuclei such as carbon, which is optimal for oscillation experiments due to its well‑characterized cross‑sections. This capability forms the basis for the Near Detector design of the DUNE experiment, currently under active development at Fermilab's Twin Pulse Test Beam Facility (FPTBF). Initial results from a first run in early 2023 are presented here, reporting the detection of protons within a neutral beam and outlining strategies for future improvements using carbon‑rich targets and accumulated data exposure.

Imitation learning has emerged as a significant avenue for robot trajectory generation, drawing inspiration from human acquisition of skills. A leading approach in this field, known as Generalized Motor Primitives (GAMP), utilizes an elastic, periodic framework augmented with Gaussian random fluctuations to recreate learned behaviors. A primary drawback of GAMP is its reliance on precise temporal alignment between training and execution, a constraint that limits real-world applicability. Existing extensions attempting to incorporate flexible temporal shaping failed to provide a corresponding learning mechanism for adapting to this adaptability. This study introduces Extended Kernelized Movement Primitives with Temporal Basis Functions (E-KTB), a flexible and learnable model designed to generate flexible-shaping trajectories. The approach represents discrepancies between demonstrated and current states via a kernelized filter applied to the elastic, periodic framework. By employing temporal basis functions to map task progress onto the filter state, the proposed method decouples demonstration dynamics from execution dynamics, thereby enabling seamless transition from reference to target trajectories while preserving task duration adaptability. Furthermore, a temporal rewriting algorithm is developed to learn the coefficients for these basis functions. Experimental validations across both simulated and physical environments demonstrate the effectiveness and adaptability of the proposed approach compared to existing methods.

Superconductors exhibiting mixed states of spin-orbit coupling and broken symmetry represent a captivating frontier in modern condensed matter theory, particularly when exploring the interplay between Rashba spin-orbit interaction (SOC) and intrinsic spin polarization under conditions of broken inversion symmetry. In this work, we analyze a two-dimensional SOC system under an external electric field and an increasing transverse SOC parameter, observing a transition from BCS pairing to extended $s$-wave character as SOC strength evolves. Notably, in the regime combining strong SOC and strong broken-symmetry-induced spin selection, a transition to non-mapped Bealian states occurs. This final phase is characterized by coexistence of pairs with opposite spins and opposite momenta and is attributed to the competition between the attractive interaction and the energy cost of spin-flipping against the SOC and magnetic fields; however, our findings suggest that introducing additional pairs with parallel spins and momenta can be advantageous. The South Atlantic rift basin, formed during the opening of the South Atlantic in the late Jurassic to Early Cretaceous periods, has experienced extensive sedimentation and tectonic deformation throughout its history, resulting in a complex geological structure. In this study, we have compiled a comprehensive dataset of 1200 active normal and strike-slip faults from 900 km of land-based magnetotelluric data. This dataset was then used to analyze lateral variations in fault attributes, with a focus on lithospheric architecture, crustal anisotropy, and plate boundary evolution. Results indicate that the western basin remains extensional in nature, characterized by thin, highly fragmented, and horizontally layered crust that mirrors surface structures, while the eastern basin is underpinned by ancient East African anisotropic crust that exhibits east-west electrical conductivity trends similar to surface observations. Transition zones between these domains display progressive shifts from western to eastern crustal characteristics across the mid-basin. These mid-basin findings challenge prevailing theories regarding the timing of plate coupling, the development of plate coupling, and the creation of plate coupling. Additionally, the absence of a surface expression of the lithospheric shear zone contradicts current surface-based predictions of where coupling should occur. Understanding this detailed fault architecture and the broader regional tectonic setup is essential for improving models of plate coupling and for reducing risks associated with offshore oil, gas, and cable infrastructure within the region.

Unlabeled pre-training has emerged as a powerful strategy for enhancing various subsequent tasks when labeled data is scarce. This paper examines the reasons behind the high false positive rate in Visual Relationship Detection (VRD). The study highlights that training is impeded by an ill-equipped relationship proposal distribution, where most negative examples are straightforward to detect—often stemming from object detection inaccuracies. Consequently, complex, low-frequency proposals suffer from inadequate fitting. To mitigate the impact of false positives and address this class imbalance, we propose Spatially-Aware Balanced Negative Sampling (SBNS). This method balances negative sampling weights based on their geographical coherence with the corresponding bounding box proposals. We also address the rarity of high-frequency regions to refine estimation accuracy. Spatially Aware Balanced Negative Sampling also involves Spatially Balanced Negative Proposals (SBNS).

We describe a strategy for conducting supervised action recognition under dark conditions. In this research, we evaluate our methods on the ARID dataset. Unlike prior investigations limited to large-scale, well-lit datasets such as Kinetics or HMDB51, our approach maintains a very low error rate despite being trained exclusively on a comparatively smaller set of dark videos. Additionally, we investigate various training and inference techniques, including domain adaptation, and introduce a practical yet simple frame selection mechanism. Experimental outcomes confirm that our model improves upon the previously published baselines by a percentage of 11%.

The presence of these non-hydrodynamic modes in this context mirrors their feature in holographic fluids, thereby bolstering the feasibility of applying hydrodynamic models to scenarios coupling fluids with gravitaton radiation.

Streaming anomaly detection involves identifying irregular data points within continuous data streams, a task that challenges both traditional and deep learning methods through issues like concept drift and the need for continuous adaptation. Leading existing algorithms often employ fixed-memory techniques such as hashing or nearest neighbors, which fail to effectively constrain rapid high-frequency values analogous to moving averages or eliminate seamless anomalies; furthermore, they cannot support end-to-end training. This study introduces an incremental approach to anomaly detection that combines random Fourier features with quantum-inspired density estimation mechanisms reminiscent of continuous exponential moving averages. Capable of handling infinite data streams while maintaining constant $O(1)$ update complexity, a comprehensive evaluation comparing the new model against twelve state-of-the-art algorithms using eighteen datasets demonstrates these results.

This research demonstrates that for any system with a security issue, there exists at least one adversarial strategy ensuring the respondent's denial of knowledge that the password is correct, even if they know it. Conversely, for specific types of systems referred herewith, there is an opposing argument involving the admission that they do know the password. This implies the application of the foreseeable conclusion doctrine would result in requiring the respondent to provide the password without risk of perjury. Nevertheless, there is also demonstration of the existence of systems that require modification to enable the respondent to safely disclose their knowledge of the password to an interrogator who understands the protocol.

We introduce a general model for simulating measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution (MDI-QKD). The rapid development of machine learning, particularly in Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) which excel at processing tabular data and extracting patterns from graphs, has sparked both significant achievements and intense debate. Key challenges include the need for user-deployable models that adhere to privacy regulations, as well as critical applications in finance, transportation, and healthcare—areas where stakes involve human safety—that demand transparency and accountability with respect to decisions impacting individuals. Consequently, it is essential for applications involving high-consequence outcomes that deep neural networks can be interpreted within the context of privacy restrictions; however, most existing explainability methods prioritize model accuracy over privacy preservation. Specifically, we demonstrate how nodes, edges, graphs (through variational dimension reduction), and latent dimensions can be identified as influential. We validate the applicability of this approach to diverse graphs autoencoding tasks that integrate privacy concerns.

Rapidly circulating through social media on a global scale, fake news threatens users and entire communities, especially as it emerges with alarming speed. While deep learning models excel when trained extensively on data for specific events, their effectiveness often declines due to domain shifts when encountering new topics. Consequently, current detection methods face major obstacles when dealing with emergent fake news events, where a lack of clean, verified training data is a critical issue. Although crowdsourcing offers a potential solution for obtaining labeled data, it introduces inherent noise that existing models are poorly equipped to handle. To solve these challenges, a new framework called Self-training for Domain Adaptation (SDA) is proposed to continuously adjust detectors for new events using noisy crowdsourced data without retraining from scratch. First, initial pseudo-labels for recently occurred events are generated based on historical similarities, serving as a foundation for self-training. Second, domain adaptation techniques bridge the gap between historical datasets and new, noisy crowdsourced inputs to enhance detection accuracy. Third, a dedicated regularization loss specifically targets common errors in identifying misinformation. Experimental results indicate that this self-supervised approach significantly surpasses existing methods in detecting fake news on emerging events.

Data rates in massive machine-type communication environments can be significantly boosted by leveraging the geographical data rates of individual machines, a concept known as macro-diversity. However, realizing this requires coordinated movement of connected machines, which in turn depends on effective data rate assignment strategies. Traditional approaches using mean field games often fail to capture the granular interactions between specific machines and critical infrastructure, such as how individual access points relate to specific devices. Therefore, this paper introduces a novel mean field formulation where access rate allocation defines the game's infrastructure, enabling the analysis of how these relationships influence system behavior. The study examines an environmental data collection scenario where a set of game-theoretic assignments drives coordinated autonomous robots (astrobots). Key properties and the equilibrium of the proposed model are investigated through a series of examples and simulations, demonstrating that these fine-grained target assignments fundamentally alter stables states and characterize fundamental system properties more profoundly than coarse mean field approximations.

GP 2 is a rule-based programming language designed to assist with verification and program analysis by utilizing transformation methods to facilitate computation. However, applications that are efficient in GP 2 face performance bottlenecks because the cost of performing graph matching is high. To overcome this challenge, GP 2 introduces rooted rules, a feature that allows certain patterns and their corresponding transformations to have their matches and updates precalculated and stored. This paper describes the syntax and semantic structure of those specific rules implemented within the language, while also explaining an algorithm designed for their execution.

Feature extraction offers a viable strategy to mitigate dimensionality challenges within high-dimensional datasets. As a prevalent self-supervised learning technique, contrastive learning has recently attracted substantial interest. In this research, we introduced a unified framework grounded in a novel interpretation of contrastive learning, applicable to both unsupervised and supervised feature extraction tasks. The framework first establishes two contrastive (CL) graphs to distinctly identify positive and negative pairs; subsequently, the projection matrix is obtained by minimizing the corresponding contrastive loss function to integrate information from both similar and dissimilar examples for unifying unsupervised and supervised extraction processes. Specifically, we detail three methodologies: one unsupervised CL approach, along with two supervised CL variants. Extensive numerical tests across five real-world datasets highlight the framework's superior performance relative to state-of-the-art methods.

Model selection or sparse modeling challenges arise frequently with categorical inputs; yet, existing literature largely overlooks categorical structures because the exponential growth of possible model configurations as the number of variables increases. This paper introduces a graphical Bayesian Lasso tailored for categorical data designed to address models with high dimensionality or sparsity. It also explores alternative encoding schemes that allow for sparse or over-parameterized models to be selected effectively within a categorical context. Simulation studies as well as a practical application to the Hubble dataset are used to evaluate the proposed methodologies, demonstrating the efficacy of these approaches in identifying accurate model structures among extensive candidate options efficiently, particularly in capturing sparse features.

This review examines spatially nonlocal diffusion models with interactions confined to a finite range determined by a positive parameter $\delta$ within a bounded domain, addressing formulations tailored to inhomogeneous data. As $\delta$ approaches zero, yielding a local limit, we analyze their consistency with inhomogeneous boundary-value problems arising from classical partial differential equations. Simultaneously, we explore results proving convergence in the asymptotic limits $\delta \to \infty$, which capture inhomogeneous data with "remote" influences. Supporting these technical findings are illustrative applications connecting nonlocal models to fractional operators and image processing contexts.

During the alignment of cameras along a vertical column, gravity often causes them to drift from the true vertical, resulting in poorly calibrated azimuth angles. Consequently, this section describes an experiment testing the efficacy of a gravity-assisted vertical calibration method for panoramic image stitching. The study involved nine colleagues aligning their cameras on a mast at the MIT CSAIL lab, with data processed to determine the force required to shift the rig away from vertical. MongoDB is widely recognized as a general-purpose, distributed, document-based NoSQL database. It offers transaction support across three distinct deployment configurations: single-document transactions driven by the WiredTiger engine on standalone nodes; multi-document transactions handled within replica sets (comprising primary and secondary nodes); and distributed transactions managed in sharded clusters (composed of multiple replicas sets). A primary issue with existing formal verification methods for MongoDB is that most models focus exclusively on either the replica set or the cluster environment, ignoring the integrity of the others. Even within specific configurations, many models fail to support the complete transaction protocol; for instance, some models of the replica set variant omit order-of-operation consistency or atomicity guarantees. This letter introduces the first formal process-algebraic model using TCS extensions of Milonin's approach, addressing all three deployment architectures and fully specifying the underlying engine protocol to fit within a unified algebraic framework. Consequently, this work provides the foundational basis for verifying various MongoDB implementations and facilitates the formal comparison of models across these deployments.
