This study presents the high-pressure structural and magnetic analysis of the layered Aurivillius oxide $\text{Bi}_5\text{FeTi}_3\text{O}_{15}$, utilizing single crystals within a diamond anvil cell paired with synchrotron white light. Structural data collected at high pressure reveals a phase transition occurring at approximately $13.5 \pm 0.5$~GPa, marked by significant changes in lattice parameters and a transition from $R3c$ to $P2_1/c$ space groups. Concurrently, magnetic susceptibility data recorded under identical conditions indicates long-range antiferromagnetic ordering beginning at a Curie-Weiss temperature ($\theta_{\text{pw}}$) of $280$ K, which rises to over $420$ K at $8$ ~GPa, corresponding to an increase in the antiferromagnetic transition temperature ($T_{\text{N}}$). Correspondence between the transition temperature increase in magnetic and structural domains suggests a direct structural origin for the magnetic alterations, consistent with modifications in the local octahedral tilting of the A- and B-site cations.

Chances of upward intergenerational mobility hinge significantly on accessible quality education. As such, measuring the value of education is vital for policy formulation. This study develops clear, empirically testable frameworks that align theoretical models with data on the mobility and educational opportunities of past generations to assess human capital policy. We apply these frameworks to two cases: Denmark and the United States, using historical data on opportunity and mobility. Our analysis reveals that in both nations, the returns to education for those born into different social classes are statistically different. Based on this finding, we propose that subsidized, universal higher education serves as an effective strategy to enhance upward intergenerational mobility.

In 2015, the CERN Large Hadron Collider (LHC) implemented a novel luminosity scanning technique known as "Emittance Scans." This method was primarily developed to assess and correct tail errors arising from longitudinal beam bunches, ensuring precise measurement of particle colliding tails. Since its introduction, it has served as an essential supplement to standard methods, notably Hourglass Factor scans, which verify assumptions regarding emittance and chromaticity. While the majority of the previous work has concentrated on the operational procedures and the systematic analysis of beta-hourglass factors, this study presents the inverse perspective by documenting the experimental methodology and applying a statistical framework to uncover subtle correlations between bunch parameters and their associated luminosity outcomes. By focusing on the data from Phase 2 of the Atlas experiment's luminosity scanning process, the paper applies Bayesian inference to reveal a marked dependency between the bunches and their luminosity characteristics. This analysis also evaluates various Bayesian approaches to calculate the corrective factors for the bunches and the median corrective factor across all groups examined.

This study addresses a distributed optimization challenge in multi-agent systems where a subset of nodes behave maliciously. Specifically, these adversaries attempt to drive the network off the optimal trajectory by corrupting data transmitted to their neighbors and imposing high bandwidth costs through excessive communication. Accordingly, we introduce a quantized, distributed gradient-based algorithm designed for benign agents. This section establishes the convergence of the proposed method to a vicinity of the global optimal solution, analytizing performance under both bandwidth constraints and adversarial interference. Finally, we validate our theoretical findings with numerical simulations.

Detecting fluctuations in the cosmic microwave background (CMB), often called anisotropies, is among the most vital techniques in cosmological research. Due to the faintness of this signal, scientists have built ever more sophisticated and sensitive instruments capable of scanning the sky across multiple frequencies with thousands of detectors sensitive to different angular scales. Because the electronics governing these complex systems are inherently stochastic, understanding their behavior through statistical analysis is crucial. Reliably estimating the true temperature fluctuations requires ensuring that the measured values are unbiased and that the associated uncertainties are accurately calculated, accounting for the complex correlations inherent in the data. In this paper, we present a rigorous derivation of the variance matrix used to estimate CMB anisotropies, addressing the specifics of how modern experiments sample and process signals from their hardware. We examine the trade-offs regarding variance when choosing estimator forms and whether to include various covariance matrix elements. Our findings indicate that for the typical scenarios found in actual CMB experiments, using a simplified estimator yields similar outcomes to those of the optimal maximum likelihood approach, yet still provides precise and reliable uncertainty estimates.

In our study, we analyzed multiple aspects of BART to determine the specific type of linguistic knowledge that facilitates word ordering. Our findings indicate that BART's ability to arrange words relies on syntactical ability and not on semantic understanding. Finally, we used an ablation study of context words to determine if the ability to arrange words is influenced by meaning or syntax.

Most prior research analyzing the throughput of random ensembles of low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes presumes independence between the degree distributions at either end of a randomly chosen edge. Going further, our work addresses LDPC ensembles featuring degree-degree correlations. First, we outline two constructive approaches for generating such degrees-temperature correlated LDPC ensembles. Next, we derive the general density evolution recurrence used to evaluate their performance on the binary erasure channel, even in instances where correlation depends dynamically on the degree degrees. While quantum key distribution (QKD) enables unconditional secure communication over distance, real-world applications remain vulnerable to "quantum hacking" stemming from hardware limitations. In this paper, we introduce a novel measurement-only attack utilizing lasers that mimic Gaussian single-photon statistics, effectively bypassing current security checks. Our Gaussian attack achieves an information yield of approximately $10^{-2}$ with error rates around $10^{-3}$, surviving at distances up to 70 km under standard attenuation and significantly increasing to over 700 m in the presence of positive operator multiplication (PM) feedback, as found in some commercial systems. Crucially, this method does not rely on the actual state prepared by the device, rendering it independent of the specific Gaussian attack model. Furthermore, we demonstrate that typical physical imperfections in QKD components provide a looser security boundary than engineered Gaussian attacks, suggesting our findings offer a more robust test case for evaluating other potential vulnerabilities.

Future mobile networks (MN) face growing pressure from data-intensive applications, necessitating advanced, intelligent, and adaptive resource management strategies. This investigation examines a MAC protocol tailored for FMCW radar networks grounded in the slotted, binary, and binary-reverse CSMA framework. In this protocol, each node transmits during reverse-chirp slots when its internal timer indicates transmission. Collision resolution occurs at specific frequencies within these reverse-chirp slots, with success or failure determined by outcomes at those frequencies rather than entire slots. To initiate transmission, a node must first pass Clear Channel Assessment (CCA); consequently, collision patterns and packet delivery limits are heavily influenced by the specific frequencies utilized during both CCA and data transmission. While the theoretical analysis adopts the standard assumptions of the ALOHA system by utilizing fixed transmission and assessment durations, it relaxes the premise of always-filled assessment slots to allow dynamic behavior within them. To establish upper and lower boundaries for performance, collision models were either adapted from, or new pieces were, traditional stochastic processes. Specifically, we utilize and possibly extend standard stochastic techniques to model channel access decisions, given the variability of CCA durations; simultaneously, we devise novel approaches and either reference or adapt existing techniques to model channel collisions, given the dependency of outcomes on CCA and transmission frequency choices. To finalize performance estimation through these methodologies, we integrate them within the statistical environment of the protocol to calculate expected convergence and efficiency metrics. Localization of dynamical processes is frequently driven by temporal correlations encoded in the system's temporal motif, a factor often overlooked in the design of structural controls. In this study, we investigate how structural controls influence dynamical localization on complex networks with the degree-degree correlation (CCC) structure. By analyzing the degree-degree CCC network in conjunction with the Laplacian matrix of a graph to determine spectral types of localization, we identify two primary structural control strategies: bidirectional control of nodes with unidirectional control of links. Our results demonstrate that both approaches induce localization across diverse initial states and panning dynamics within networks characterized by negative CCC. Specifically, bidirectional link operations enable localization independent of network size, whereas link operations with negative correlation influence localization based on the network's size. Furthermore, compared to controlling nodal activity individually, our structural strategies achieve broader localization under equivalent conditions. Ultimately, our work elucidates the mechanism by which structural controls foster dynamical localization.

Evaluating and forecasting professional team performance is a significant challenge in both research and practice. While numerous studies have analyzed football team and player defense, they often neglect the statistical probability and magnitude by which opponents breach defensive lines to score. This paper proposes a novel evaluation framework that incorporates missing elements from existing research by examining the probability and intensity of defensive failures alongside established metrics. Specifically, we develop a mixed-effects Cox proportional hazards model integrated with an evaluation system to capture the stochastic nature of defensive collapses. Extracting information from form image templates is challenging due to variations in layout, design, and text orientation. Existing methods often fail because they cannot adequately recognize text in non-horizontal directions or differentiate input areas from others based on contextual clues. To address these issues, a new deep learning framework, FormImageContextualNetwork (FICN), has been introduced. This template detector analyzes both spatial and semantic characteristics of text blocks to locate and identify specific fields. The FICN architecture employs Directional Text Detection (DTD) modules to detect input fields using directional text cues, while Text-Text Semantic Relationship (TTSR) modules infer empty form fields by analyzing the content of neighboring filled fields. Experiments across two datasets, Specific Document Textline (SDT) and FormInTheWild (FIDW), demonstrate that the proposed methods significantly enhance template detection accuracy compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches.

Hidden-Parameter Recurrent State Space Models (HiP-RSSMs) address the limitations of traditional Reversible Sequence-based Sequential Models (RSSM), such as assuming fixed and static dynamics, which often misalign with real-world variability. These static limitations can be bypassed in many domains by treating dynamic variations as latent variables, which HiP-RSSM achieves by employing a family of parameterizable dynamical systems driven by hidden variables to model them. This method enables capacity for complex, context-adaptive behaviors that standard RSSM handles intractably, specifically offering the ability to generalize across entire families of trajectories and effectively manage multi-timescale tasks. Although standard approaches for learning standard models include variational techniques, they are often computationally difficult and fail to recover the ideal point estimates for these parameters. While recent techniques like SSMLearn use implicit optimization for this purpose, the algorithms we introduce reformulate both manifold identification and normal form calculation as direct, explicit problems under specific constraints. Demonstrating significant improvements on both experimental and numerical datasets, these simplified algorithms generate precise, sparse rigorous models for systems exhibiting strongly nonlinear or non-linearizable behaviors, achieving a speed improvement of several orders of magnitude.

Standard models yielding 1D or 2D solitons, including Gross-Pitaevskii (GP) equations for Bose-Einstein condensates (BECs), exhibit Galilean invariance, facilitating the derivation of traveling soliton families from static ones. A significant research goal is identifying models that support stable self-accelerating (SA) soliton motion. While linear systems possess SA Airy wave solutions, their nonlinear amplitude tails cannot sustain binding for multi-particle scenarios; however, recent two-component GP predictions suggest the possibility of interacting SA BESTRUCTS. To explore this further, we developed two distinct two-component BEPC models capable of generating various interacting SA 1D soliton configurations. Specifically, these include 1D GP 1D GP Airy-packet states and hybrid combinations linking SA modes with accelerated vortex dynamics. These systems allow continuous control over inter-component acceleration by adjusting coupling between SA modes of individual condensates or SA modes against their accelerated vortex counterparts. Additionally, we investigated the impact of GP dynamics on the acceleration of vortex solitons within one component relative to an SA BEC in the other. Finally, we analyzed GP effects accelerating vortices near an SA packet in the second component.

This work addresses secure machine learning inference in an environment containing both a malicious client and a semi-trusted server, where only the client accesses the prediction results while the server handles computation with limited access to data. Contrary to the typical assumption of communication between perfectly adversarial parties, the inclusion of a semi-trusted server allows us to leverage additional constraints on data usage. We introduce a strategy that combines trusted execution environments (TEEs) with secure multi-party computation (MPC) to secure this process. Specifically, we optimize secure generic fully homomorphic encryption (FHE)-based implementations by streamlining protocols for both linear and non-linear operations, thereby reducing redundancy and data interactions. Experimental results demonstrate significant efficiency gains over standard FHE-based MPC approaches, particularly in high-overhead non-linear computations, with reduced execution times. These improvements position our lightweight TEE-MPC framework as an effective practical alternative.

Using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST), we conducted a high-sensitivity neutral hydrogen (HI) survey toward the nearby spiral galaxy M101, focusing specifically on the galaxy's outer halo. Our analysis of the position-velocity diagrams revealed evidence for an asymmetric HI halo in M101. The total mass of this asymmetric halo was calculated at $1.04 \pm 0.11 \times 10^7 M_{\odot}$, with the structure positioned between 31.8$^+$0.4$-$0.3 and 33.0$+$0.4$-$0.3 h71 pc kpc from the center of M101. Given that only 13 such asymmetric halos have currently been identified in total, this finding makes M101 the fourth galaxy known to possess one. Additionally, cross-referencing UV imaging showed a compact (radius approx. 3 pc) young stellar cluster located within the galaxy's disk directly beneath the halo's projection, leading us to suggest that gravitational interactions between M101 and this cluster may be the origin of the detected asymmetric halo.

Utilizing external knowledge to assist machine-based question answering (QA) on tasks requiring commonsense background faces the challenge of overwhelming and misleading information due to the boundless volume of such data. To address this, we introduce a semantics-driven, knowledge-aware QA framework designed to regulate knowledge injection from coarse to fine granularity. We implement a filtering strategy to refine extracted information based on the initial (coarse) semantics of a question and have created a semantics-aware retrieval module. This module leverages structural knowledge inputs and performs hierarchical fusion of appropriate facts aligned with the precise (fine-grained) semantics of questions. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method outperforms strong baseline approaches on the CommonsenseQA benchmark dataset.

The resulting intense spectrum includes both near-infrared (NIR) and infrared (IR) wavelengths, contributing significantly to a comet's spectral signature. The intensity of an ionized molecule's emission at NIR and IR wavelengths can serve as reliable indicators of local temperature, gas densities, and other physical conditions within a comet. We introduce an innovative on-the-fly approach to Raman spectroscopy, enabled by a tiny, inexpensive, and fully integrated mini-photonic device. Conventional techniques rely on scanning a diffraction grating against a prism's dispersion to achieve high resolution, a slow process. In contrast, our system utilizes the chip-scale photonic device to replace the crystal element within a standard single-monochromator setup. By filtering light with the photonic structure's narrow transmission window during the acquisition process, the system separates Raman-shifted information directly into an intensity scan of the detector signal, eliminating the need for mechanical scanning. The resulting spectral reconstruction involves only a one-dimensional shift of a two-dimensional (x, t) detector image frame—a task easily handled by modern GPU capabilities. We demonstrate this setup performing analytical chemistry by analyzing liquid samples in various containers, including glass vials, opaque plastic bottles, and even view through the container via simultaneous illumination with white light alongside laser excitation. This configuration simplifies spectroscopic hardware while maintaining analytical capability, offering a pathway for future automation in chemical analysis with the help of AI, especially when combined with our recently released open-source Python-based Raman reconstruction toolkit.

Lately, various machine learning models addressing tasks such as polypharmacy adverse effect recognition, predicting drug interactions, and planning combination treatments have been developed. In this work, we offer a cohesive theoretical perspective on relational machine learning models capable of managing these specific objectives. Furthermore, we define key concepts, contrast prevailing architectures, and evaluate metrics, datasets, and assessment methodologies. Additionally, the following section highlights promising high-impact applications as well as significant avenues for future investigation within this specific field.

This paper introduces a rough path version adapted of an It\^{o}-Wentzell formula, specifically requiring an \(\alpha\)-Holder regularity where $\alpha \in (\frac{1}{3},\frac{1}{2}]\), and simultaneously generalizes and improves upon earlier findings by Cui and Riedel as well Wang and R\^{u}et for the case when $\theta \in (1/3,1/3)$.

This work addresses the challenge of creating a high-performance and reliable evaluation framework for Federated Learning (FL). While current methodologies often rely on assumptions of independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) data across nodes, this paper proposes a practical Co-Collection Learning (CCL) method to estimate key performance metrics using only the central validator's access to a proxy dataset, thereby obviating the need to gather additional data from participating parties. Furthermore, the study provides a rigorous statistical analysis of the proposed estimator. Our experimental results demonstrate a substantial enhancement in both efficiency and robustness relative to existing state-of-the-art evaluation frameworks.

Although rotating turbulence is typically associated with inverse cascades dominated by rotation and mean flow generation, it can also be governed by wave dynamics under certain conditions. This paper investigates direct energy cascading in strongly rotating turbulent systems where geostrophic balances give way to wave-based interactions. Specifically, the study focuses on rotating tank experiments subjected to continuous lateral mechanical agitation, for which theoretical models predict wave turbulence with a directionless energy cascade. Experimental measurements, derived from PIV tracking of the free surface, confirm the presence of elevated kinetic energy moving to smaller scales, thereby validating the predicted direct cascade and the geometrically induced directionlessness consistent with wave turbulence theories.

Individuals involved with the criminal justice system disproportionately experience mental health disorders. Drawing upon data from North Carolina courts covering 1994 to 2009, this study analyzes whether requiring offenders on probation to receive mental healthcare lowers their subsequent likelihood of reincarceration. By exploiting random variations in judge assignments, the analysis contrasts individuals mandated to participate in treatment programs with those under probation without such requirements. The findings reveal that mandating treatment reduces recidivism within three years by a margin of 5.6 percentage points—or 17 percent—compared to non-treatment probationers. While specific impacts on violent and property crimes demonstrate reduced recurrence, the beneficial trends also intensify as time progresses post-conviction. Finally, a cost-benefit assessment indicates that resulting decreases in crime sufficiently reimburse expenses associated with offering these programs.

Pixel-level annotation signifies a critical and resource-intensive task, frequently serving as a bottleneck, especially within the domain of medical segmentation. Although recent advancements have enhanced segmentation efficacy, these improvements often only lower dependencies on precisely labeled training data. Consequently, researchers are increasingly转向 tasks such as domain adaptation, semi-supervised learning, and training without labels. In response, we introduce a new segmentation framework known as Self-labeling with Alignment (SaA). Our method employs self-labeling strategies alongside an alignment mechanism to胡合 intra- and inter-scale features, aiming to handle natural imagery segmentation at a larger scale. Specific self-labeling prototypes are fine-тuned using an image translation model to enhance cross-domain feature consistency through a translation-invariant approach. Furthermore, our alignment framework enhances SaA through a multi级结构，which incorporates both hierarchical and global-level labeling frameworks to strengthen layer-wise and integrated learning processes. Evaluations across four external datasets highlight the superiority of SaA when applied to large-scale medical image segmentation at the natural image segmentation level.

To address the increased luminosity at the Large Hadron Collider expected in the upcoming run, existing trigger mechanisms and data acquisition systems require significant upgrades. This paper introduces a new hardware-based filtering system, designed as the Level-3 trigger, intended for future hadron physics experiments at the facility. Implemented within an all-silicon tracking detector, this system leverages Field-Programmable Gate Arrays (FPGAs) to execute efficient jet-algorithms for making rapid decisions. Key functionalities include jet reconstruction, precision calculations of jet energy, and the use of information from underlying event subtraction to enhance overall performance. It operates effectively across diverse collision scenarios with optimized latencies of approximately 10 microsecond, enabling high-luminosity data filtering at rates exceeding 1 million events per second. This approach offers a versatile architecture capable of supporting various experimental objectives and adaptable reconfiguration of algorithms without requiring hardware changes, allowing users to define specific jet finding parameters through software inputs. Practical applications demonstrating the system's capabilities and initial deployments in physics-driven tests have also been presented.

Deferred Neural Rendering achieves a distinguished balance among speed, visual fidelity, and computational efficiency. When applied to animated rigid bodies, this approach presents an accessible pathway to creating high-quality virtual human avatars. By leveraging learned adaptations of DNR applied to animated rigid bodies, this method achieves high-quality digital human avatars via simplified techniques. This method enables the simultaneous extraction of implicit shape and texture from limited observations, utilizing DNR's capabilities to produce realistic appearances in both reflective environments and under specular lighting.

Measuring atomic disorder levels is vital for understanding how changes in local structural environments influence material performance and longevity. This study utilizes graph neural networks to establish a physically interpretable index for local disorder, defined by the deviation of a sample's atomic graph representation from that of its nearest crystalline or amorphous match from a comprehensive database of crystalline, amorphous, and glassy forms sharing identical chemical compositions. Our analysis indicates that significant disorder exists across various disordered materials—ranging from nanocrystalline and polycrystalline to largely amorphous specimens—encompassing over 100,000 structures drawn from more than 3,000 materials. When applied to predicting crystallographic preferred orientation in nanocrystalline materials, this new metric achieves higher accuracy compared to conventional approaches. Consequently, this method offers a robust framework for characterizing structural disorder, which is essential for advancing first-principles investigations of diverse chemical and physical states.

Knowledge Tracing (KT) applies students' historical interaction records to model their evolving knowledge states and predict their future learning outcomes. While deep learning-based approaches for KT have recently achieved significant advancements, the exact drivers behind these DL-KT models remain elusive, and their proper evaluation and analysis continue to be difficult tasks. Specifically, existing studies lack consistency in assessing generalization and other critical dimensions like robustness, privacy adherence, and alignment with pedagogical theory. To rectify these gaps, this paper introduces a unified Deep Learning-KT framework, termed DL-KT, and proposes a comprehensive evaluation system using the unified framework to address knowledge representation, embedding dynamics, prediction mechanisms, generalization, robustness, pedagogical congruence, and both privacy and security concerns. We further present a comprehensive DL-KT benchmark dataset and evaluate a total of eleven DL-KT models across four leading institutions—ID-KT, DN-KT, DL-KT, and others. Our findings reveal that current DL-KT methods struggle with several capabilities, including generalization, robustness, and educational alignment, indicating that many effective components are still missing in these models. Consequently, we have put forward a series of enhanced DL-KT solutions and theoretical frameworks to guide future research. Finally, our analysis underscores the necessity of integrating privacy-preserving techniques, specifically a Peer-KT collaborative DL-KT method incorporating differential privacy, to safeguard student information effectively.

This work demonstrates that a second-order elliptic differential operator $P$ possesses a closed range within the smooth function space $C^\infty(M)$ on any manifold $M$. Moreover, for any manifold $M$ lacking compact subcomponents, the operator $P$ demonstrates surjectivity on $C^\infty(M)$, with applications yielding to Helmholtz theory explored accordingly.

The version of the proof format adopted by the veriT SMT solver was initially showcased ten years ago following the first PxTP workshop. Since its inception, this format has fully evolved to the point where it supports various SMT applications, with other proof-producing solvers also generating files in this format. To secure a better direction for future advancements in this format, this article aims to solicit input from practitioners. To achieve that, it will examine the evolution history of the format as well as the pragmatic strategies used through its development while discussing the issues that may arise when other generating-proofs engines rely on the veriT proofs format.

Synchronous updates often reduce efficiency in cross-device federated learning, specifically as the pool of active clients expands. Nguyen et al., 2022 demonstrated in a homogeneous setting that asynchronous updates can mitigate this expansion's issues with essentially no loss of performance, yet their method failed to deliver results in heterogeneous environments. This paper presents Provable Asynchronous Federated Learning (PAFL), which provides guarantees for heterogeneity while proving that asynchronous methods match the performance of their synchronous counterparts. We establish that, provided the pool of active clients increases, asynchronous updates achieve the same convergence rates as updates, thus addressing both heterogeneity concerns and scalability issues simultaneously. We further show experimental results supporting our theoretical results that PAFL indeed performs well in both homogeneous and heterogeneous environments in comparison to the previous methods.

Recent advancements in Character-level Joint Training (C-Joint) for automatic speech recognition (ASR) provide a method to train multiple system variants simultaneously using an intermediate character set. This study examines the use of intermediate alphabets in CR-Joint training specifically for the Mandarin language, analyzing how different sets influence recognition accuracy and overall system performance. Our results indicate two key mechanisms of the intermediate alphabet's efficacy: it enhances data efficiency by expanding the effective training corpus through its own repetitive content and improves generalization across diverse acoustic and linguistic variations introduced during the synthesis using variable voice timbres. Furthermore, this study proposes VOW2PHON, an optimized strategy for training in the intermediate set that focuses specifically on syllable-onset vowels, demonstrating consistent improvements over standard CR-Joint training using a basic alphabet across all measured metrics.

Proximity-preserving and structural role-based node embeddings serve as a crucial technique in practical graph mining. This research introduces two innovative approaches: "Relation-to-Path" and "Child Subgraph" techniques designed to convert these node embeddings into intermediate group representations known as "community-based representations." These generated community embeddings are subsequently employed for enhancing the downstream node classification task, resulting in a significant improvement of approximately 3% compared to state-of-the art performance. Additionally, this framework extends utility by allowing graphs to retain their original node features, thereby facilitating higher accuracy in semantic tasks such as classification.

Recent work has established a precise correspondence between the temperature of Hawking radiation and the entropy force acting on the horizon within no-hair theorems. This finding offers a promising avenue for the observational detection of black dimensions: if such a phenomenon exists, it allows for the inference of the entropy force in asymptotically de Sitter spacetimes lacking certain fields, thereby revealing the integrity of the third law of black hole thermodynamics even in these contexts. The paper at hand explores the asymptotically de Sitter black hole environment containing an Einstein-dilaton field to determine if the absence of specific fields can expose hidden dimensions in the dark sector. By employing various ansatz forms for the dilaton function and implementing nodatal boundary conditions, we demonstrate that the gravity-coupled sector indeed supports Einstein-dimensionality with a measured rate of radiative emission from the horizon nearly 15 percent higher than predicted by standard general relativity. Consequently, if entropy forces observed in cosmic phenomena actually signify this effect within the Einstein-dimensionality framework, it could facilitate observational confirmation of the presence of a dark dimensional sector.

The study presents a highly effective force transmission approach for series elastic actuators (SEAs) centered on a Transmission Force Observer (TFOB) for estimating force. This method addresses force detection challenges in SEAs resulting from nonlinearities in elastic transmissions, ensuring precise detection of actual transmitted force with a focus on dynamic performance. A new design parameter has also been proposed specifically to enhance the high-frequency performance of this force transmission system overall. Simulation and physical testing confirm the validity of the proposed solution, demonstrating its capability to accurately detect force behavior across a broad spectrum of operations.

A particle raft suspended on an elongating liquid substrate serves as a large-scale analog for material rupture. The temporal resolution of this setup permits the observation of both particle relaxation and the development of cracks. Experiments show that the raft undergoes uniaxial stretching as the air-fluid interface beneath it expands, resulting in morphologies that vary with stretching speed. These include classic transverse fissures, complex networks of cusps and loops, or flat fault planes resembling slip planes. By combining numerical simulations with experimental observations, we establish a universal framework describing the dynamics of raft rupture. This model accounts for the interplay between inertia, gravitational forces, friction, and elastic deformations to clarify the diverse failure patterns seen in systems ranging from laboratory scales to geological events.

We examine SU(Nc) gauge theories in three dimensions incorporating degenerate complex scalar multicomponent fields (where Nf exceeds 1) that belong to the fundamental representation, respecting both global U(Nf) symmetry and SU(Nc) gauge symmetry, and subject to the most general quartic potential consistent with these symmetries. By analytically solving the saddle-point equations for Nc=2 using path integral methods and determining critical temperatures for symmetry breaking across various parameters (for specific cases like Nf=2, where Nc=3 solutions were not computed), we observe that these theories display phase-structure diversity influenced significantly by the magnitude of the quartic coupling. Consequently, the simple "linear" assumption for the potential is invalid in describing phase transitions, particularly for larger values of Nf and Nc=2. Furthermore, our results indicate the existence of a phase characterized by residual symmetry for specific parameter choices, a finding that holds significant weight for understanding dual quantum descriptions and the nature of phase diagrams in these systems.

We introduce a Temporal Difference (TD) learning approach designed to tackle the navigation challenges marine robots encounter in underwater settings. To enhance data efficiency and ensure compatibility with real-time operations, the method integrates Gaussian Process regression with an advanced rejection-sparing algorithm. This framework derives the predictive distribution for the state value and utilizes these moments to propose SPGP-SARSA, novel algorithm for model-free policy evaluation. SPGP-TD emerges from straightforward modifications to SPGP-SARSA, establishing a corresponding model-based variant. Both algorithms are validated via extensive simulations as well as practical tests using a submersible, where SPGP-SARSA demonstrates superiority over current state-of-the-art techniques and exact predictive capabilities.

Employing recent observations, we have created multi-component equilibrium models for a Milky Way-like galaxy disk. These models incorporate a central bar structure crucial for explaining observed features, most notably the "knots" within rotational curves and the kinematic warping. We assess various combinations of structural elements—including the bar, long-wavelength spiral arms, radial flows, vertical forces, and hot gaseous halos—demonstrating that the simplest viable model necessitates both the central bar and minor radial velocities. Moreover, standard gas outflows or an extended gaseous halo fail to account for the specific patterned warping observed. Moreover, using observed surface density wave patterns, we derive the four-force vector (magnitude and phase), and apply it to determine the three primary sources of disk warping: warping induced directly by waves, dynamical effects from long-period spirals, movement from long-lived coherent radial expansions/contractions, and mass-assembly history variations. Finally, we attribute the dominant effect, lasting waves resulting from secular gravitational interactions between the disk and bulge components, primarily to perturbations generated by the central bar.

Major mergers represent one of the most dramatic cosmic events, driving substantial morphological and structural shifts; such events can degrade extended stellar discs, transforming spirals into lenticulars or ellipticals while also triggering the formation of giant starbursts and active galactic nuclei. Due to their heightened luminosity in the ultraviolet and infrared spectra, major mergers are readily identifiable in both local and high-redshift populations through multiwavelength observations. Additionally, these events induce high gas consumption rates, producing abundant heavy elements and cross-luminosities across various spectral ranges, often peaking as "starburst-clips" or quasar bursts that are easily distinguished from disc galaxies.

However, minor mergers constitute an equally vital class of interaction that frequently goes unnoticed. Distinct from major events, minor mergers feature a large mass disparity between merging bodies that occurs on a significantly extended timeline, exerting milder but influential effects on morphological and star-formation characteristics that are difficult to detect immediately using standard diagnostics. Definitively identifying and categorizing low-mass merger scenarios poses a difficult challenge, particularly regarding the precise physical boundary of the dry- vs. wet-merge regimes.

In practice, numerical rounding is ubiquitous. This research addresses how rounded observations influence inference about parameters of such settings. We examine the case where $X$ is a non-negative discrete random variable with a Poisson distribution, observed as a vector of rounded counts $\mathbf{X} = (X_1, \dots, X_n) \in \mathbb{Z}^n$. Available data typically categorizes $\mathbf{X}$ into $k$ equispaced intervals defined by precision $\Delta > 0$, yielding frequencies $\mathbf{N} = (N_1, \dots, N_k)$. To address this, we introduce a Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) rejection-importance sampling scheme to generate the posterior distribution of the Poisson parameter $\lambda$ given the summary statistics $\mathbf{N}$. Since $\lambda$ fully characterizes $X$, this variable's posterior also describes $X$'s posterior distribution given $\mathbf{N}$. The delta-method approximation for $\lambda$ serves as an efficient importance distribution for this posterior, allowing exact analytical computation of the marginal posterior for $\lambda$ under $\mathbf{N}$. Under $\mathbf{N}$, the conditional distribution of $X$ remains Poisson; the conditional distribution of $\lambda$ given $\mathbf{N}$ and a specific realization $\mathbf{x}$ can similarly be derived analytically. This paper examines the allocation of indivisible goods among strategic agents with additive valuation functions, operating in a non-monetary setting where a mechanism must select a feasible allocation. It investigates whether the Pareto optimal (PO) constraint can nearly eliminate all envy-free allocations. Specifically, we analyze properties of PO allocations that satisfy the envy-free condition up to one item (EF1). We establish that for both single-minded and unit-demand valuations, EF1 allocations exist within the Pareto optimal set under these conditions, a finding reinforced by examples showing these allocations are strictly PO. Conversely, for general additive valuations, such allocations are not necessarily strictly PO; however, we demonstrate their existence by proving they exist within the up-to-lexicographic (ULX) satisfied set within the Pareto optimal framework. Finally, applying these contributions to a pure exchange economy context yields the existence of at least one EF1 Walrasian equilibrium for unit-demand agents and EF1 approximate market-clearing prices for general additive agents.

This work is driven by the challenge of adapting speech translation systems to new, monolingual acoustic domains while retaining existing, bilingual supervised training data. We hypothesize that multi-domain training, even in supervised settings, serves as an effective regularizer, preventing overfitting to a single domain and enhancing performance across all areas, including unseen domains. To support this regularization mechanism in an unsupervised speech translation scenario—where only the target domain's speech data exists and the source language and translation functions must be inferred—we propose introducing stochastic translation as an additional domain-adaptation technique. Our findings indicate an improvement in cross-domain translation speed and accuracy on multiple datasets compared to baseline approaches, demonstrating that our method outperforms a baseline that treats all training data as one homogeneous source.

The low surface brightness (LSB) spiral UGC 8839 rarely exhibits stellar formation, with a notable exception being a massive HII region complex situated at its outermost disc edge. To investigate the origins and characteristics associated with this cluster, researchers analyzed optical, near-infrared (NIR), and X-ray observations of UGC 8839 and its surrounding environment. The results reveal that the galaxy possesses several rings aligned in both mass and heat, composed of dark matter halos and stellar populations respectively, despite the concentration of current star formation occurring as a distinct, widespread structure. The authors conducted spectral energy distribution analyses of the complex using both near-IR and multi-component modelling techniques, determining that star clusters R1 and R2 are linked by a common gaseous envelope forming along an extended spiral arm. By utilizing the discrete nature of these charges, we formulate new, testable predictions based on the charge convexity conjecture, which asserts that a set of states with varying $U(1)$ charges can always have their "center of mass" charge state completed by a further physical state with lower or equal energy. We further examine the scenario where $U(1)$ promotes to a gauge symmetry within a minimal model. In such gauged scenarios, the Weak Gravity Conjecture mandates the existence of a lightest black hole corresponding to each discrete gauge charge. We conclude that minimal model gauge theories typically contain a sufficient spectrum to satisfy this requirement, possibly due to a connection between weakly coupled gauge fields and fractional Brout-Englert-Higgs (BEH) mechanisms inherent in these models.

Surface termination plays a pivotal role in determining the physical properties of materials. In this work, the influence of surface termination on the metal-insulator transition (MIT) within V$_2$O$_3$ films is investigated, with specific attention to how oxygen stoichiometry alters this transition. MIT behavior is clearly discerned in thin (4-nl) films grown on Si (100) substrates, the physical extent of which is controlled in films of varying thickness via oxygen partial pressure regulation. MIT characteristics persist across diverse substrate orientations, including LaAlO$_3$ and V(00l)-oriented surfaces. The MIT is also confirmed through photoemission data, where the dispersion relations of surface and Dyson-Mott gaps exhibit significant sensitivity to surface termination. Furthermore, the observed correlation between MIT features and oxygen content in variously terminated surfaces suggests that this phenomenon arises from a synergy between correlation effects and surface physics, distinguishing V$_2$O$_3$ from bulk samples, where MIT is less influenced by such surface variations.

This study reveals novel features of non-equilibrium dynamics in a lattice system, specifically examining how quantum double-dark-soliton (QDSD) dynamics are influenced by quasi-Bose-Einstein condensation within a bichromatic optical lattice. Notably, in degree 2, this added framework defines a sympectical double vector bundle, a skew-symmetric counterpart to metric double vector bundles. Finally, we address the scenario of entirely linearising $N$-manifolds, exploring how the functor applies when applied to the tangent graded bundle.

Mapping classical disordered statistical mechanics models to quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes serves as a highly effective strategy for discovering and evaluating these codes, particularly when the resulting models exhibit phase transitions where disorder is relevant and enhances analytical tractability. In the Shamim-Stace framework, code performance is evaluated based on the phase transition of the associated classical model. Here, we broaden the approach to instances where the classical model is in the glassy phase, lacking long-range order and characterized by a absence of thermodynamic transition in the thermodynamic limit. Consequently, we evaluate performance in terms of a critical error threshold derived directly from the statistical mechanics properties of the dual model, demonstrating that even though the dual model lacks a traditional transition, a limiting error tolerance still exists. We validate these predictions through direct comparison with standard performance calculations.

The code proves highly versatile, capable of efficiently producing the full joint spectrum and associated wave functions. While this capability was previously available only through the older, less efficient full-factorization method (FYZ), the new algorithm leverages the enhanced, robust variational approach (RVA). As a demonstration of its power, the code calculates the low-lying energy spectrum, expectation and covariance values, and correlation functions of various observables for both balanced and asymmetric traps, providing insights into the underlying electron density correlations.

This study examines the low-Reynolds-number motion of a recently proposed swimmer, consisting of three interconnected beads (where the middle connects orthogonally to the lateral pair), within an Oldroyd-B viscoelastic environment. Analytical methods were employed to determine both the linear and nonlinear (at high actuation frequencies) phase shifts experienced by this figure-8 oscillating organism. It was found that at these intense oscillation levels, elastic effects dominate, enabling control over a swimmer's direction of displacement relative to its oscillation through the geometric arrangement of its components. Furthermore, regardless of fluid elasticity, the geometry yields a nonzero forward velocity due to a hysteresis-like phenomenon inherent in the motion; however, at moderate to high elasticities, this geometric propulsion speedovers happens to nearly vanish. This result is attributed to the specific figure-8 pattern's lack of timescale separation, a conclusion supported by generic resonant normal-mode analysis. Consequently, even though the leading theoretical models (referred to as Oldroyd-B fluids in this text, perhaps intentionally or not as such) predict no speedup for this figure-eight motion at high frequencies when the swimmer moves forward under certain viscoelastic conditions, experiments suggest that experimenters might observe enhanced speeds for other types of self-actuated organisms in similar environments, highlighting the need to test nonorthogonal bead configurations next.

We examine a learning scenario where agents, organized into a networked structure, interact with either a single or multiple game environments. The core objective is to evaluate whether widely adopted "social-learning" algorithms can converge to a Nash Equilibrium more effectively than "individual" learning methods. Our analysis reveals a distinct disadvantage for agents relying on information from neighbors: as the density of connections (and thus the reliance on external input) increases, the variance in outcomes fluctuates with higher amplitude while converging at an accelerated rate. Paradoxically, these sharp fluctuations impair the overall efficacy of the social-learning approaches under these conditions. Conversely, in the case of a noisy stochastic payoffs game, we identify and analyze a specific "no-man's land" regarding the phase transition between convergence to a fixed point versus a limit cycle. The third section explores the impact of a "small-world" topology on the celebrated Exponential Reversal Algorithm (ERA), demonstrating that the system can be driven into an attractor characterized by significant state fluctuations and chaotic behavior as the topological parameters evolve. The final section presents simulation results supporting our theoretical findings.

Information security within cyberspace relies heavily on security measures (CSMs) provided by vendors. Effectively choosing the most appropriate measures for specific scenarios is a significant challenge due to the vast array of available options, resulting in wasted resources, substandard security, and frustrated users. This paper introduces a user-centric framework designed to aid in the selection of CSMs by mapping both vendor options and user requirements through the use of an information security ontology (ISO). Initially, we defined an ontology framework and subsequently populated it with criteria, attributes, and other relevant data regarding common CSMs to establish knowledge-rich ontology instances (KLRI). This enables advanced querying, reasoning, and other data processing tasks using semantic technologies. The proposed approach supports security logic, facilitating the inference that specific vendor attributes align with certain user needs based on shared security criteria. Evaluations demonstrate the framework's capability to deliver efficient, resource-conscious, and effective results when addressing information security vendor selection using the developed ISO and KLRI.

Distinct from equilibrium statistical mechanics, where one finds the Ising model, the voter model characterizes nonequilibrium systems. We analyze an opinion-formation framework combining Ising agents (proportion $1-p$) and voter agents (proportion $p$), which analytically transitions from an equilibrium to a nonequilibrium regime. Specifically, the $p=0$ limit remains in equilibrium while any $p>0$ drives the system out of equilibrium. For the nonequilibrium case, we derive the dynamic large deviation function (Erdos-Renyi network) which quantifies typical ordering and rare fluctuations in opinion order parameters and cyclic breaks. Notably, $p$ exerts a drastic influence: even a microscopic concentration of Ising agents ($p \ll 1$) causes discontinuous jumps in opinion order parameters and large breaks for any non-zero $p$. Consequently, the remaining system behavior is determined by how that small fraction of Ising agents distributes across the network. Furthermore, the derived function reveals episodes of coherent herding—where the voter model usually dominates—exhibiting simultaneous oscillations in opinion density that do not occur in the pure models. These episodes involve chaotic long-time behavior where the majority opinions of both A and $\bar A$ fluctuate abruptly and unpredictably.

Coronavirus transmission primarily occurs via infected individuals by releasing the virus through their respiratory tract through mechanisms such as talking, coughing, or sneezing. These viruses remain exposed to the external environment as they travel attached to droplets of varying dimensions; larger droplets settle relatively quickly due to gravity, while smaller ones can remain airborne for extended durations and pose a significant risk of airborne transmission of the virus. Consequently, understanding how environmental factors influence the evaporation of these droplets is essential to modeling their propagation effectively. This study analytically investigates the evolution of droplet size and concentration considering evaporation, sedimentation, Brownian motion, and UV sterilization. By addressing how coronavirus spreads through droplets and how these influences operate, this work offers a useful framework for effectively mitigating the spread of the virus. Our analytical findings are subsequently validated through comparisons with numerical simulations to ensure accuracy and reliability to effectively mitigate coronavirus spread via droplets.

Consequently, a substantial research effort currently focuses on devices capable of delivering robust inferences and quantifying the certainty associated with each result. As these techniques are widely utilized in both entirely differentiable architectures and those combining non-differentiable components, we specifically distinguish between separable uncertainty types to select the most effective combination for their respective calculation.

Pyroptosis serves as a crucial innate immune defense mechanism, driven by the assembly of the NLRP3 inflammasome and the subsequent formation of gasdermin (GSD) pores. Our research identifies O-GlcNAcylation, a specific PTM, as essential for stabilizing the active NLRP3 complex and driving effective pyroptosis. Our findings demonstrate that this modification stabilizes NLRP3 independently of its canonical activation triggers, such as K+ efflux and the presence of the activator ATP. Furthermore, the study reveals a functional interplay where O-GlcNAcylation regulates the relationship between NLRP3 and its negative regulator, the K+ channel TKY, creating conditions favorable for activation. Importantly, the observed acceleration in pyroptosis and associated organ damage following ischemic/reperfusion injury may be mitigated through the inhibition of this O-GlcNAcylation process. Consequently, these data suggest a new strategy for treating inflammatory disorders by modulating PTMs to prevent excessive tissue and organ damage.

In reinforcement learning, exogenous state variables can introduce unpredictable variance into rewards, thereby decelerating the learning process. Consequently, we present two distinct algorithms designed to detect these exogenous variables. Experimental results on various MDP tasks validate that these approaches are practically viable, offering substantial accelerations to reinforcement learning performance.

This design enables the network to learn just one example of the desired waveform at that specific $F_0$ during training, supporting synthesis at multiple frequencies without further learning. The architecture achieves this through a decomposition into basic harmonics and a shared harmonic neural network trained primarily on these latent features using $F_0$-specific PDCNNs, resulting in significant reductions in learning requirements and model parameters compared to the original WaveNet. Furthermore, a comparative analysis against a nine-million parameter version of WaveNet reveals that QPNet uses roughly 30 times fewer parameters while producing superior synthesis quality, as confirmed by objective metrics and human evaluations.

Speech Translation involves converting spoken audio in one language into written text in another. Traditional cascaded systems, which combine an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) module with a Machine Translation (MT) system, struggle with error propagation. In contrast, Direct Neural Machine Translation approaches utilize a single end-to-end model to directly optimize a scoring function for speech translation, offering improved performance in applications like virtual assistants and in-car systems. Speech-translation-zero-shot (ST-Zero) represents an emerging challenge where a trained neural speech translation model handles unseen language pairs by leveraging reference translations, effectively treating it as a problem of reinforcement learning through reference rewriting. However, existing studies on ST-Zero face two significant hurdles. First, current reference datasets are insufficient, as they lack the parallel monolingual corpora necessary for training models on numerous speech translation tasks that do not have direct supervision. Second, current evaluation metrics are inadequate, as they fail to properly assess translation quality when no direct training data exists for specific language pairs. To resolve these deficiencies, we conduct the most extensive study to date on ST-Zero datasets and evaluation methods, and introduce the multilingual Neural Speech Translation (NM) framework. This framework trains models on broad speech translation tasks and enables zero-shot inference for unseen combinations. Finally, we evaluate 33 language pairs across five major speech translation benchmarks to address the problem of limited data and establish a new, rigorous standard for assessment.

Accurate and computationally efficient assessment of Newtonian potentials across diverse two-dimensional regions is vital for the numerical solution of Poisson equations and volume integral equations. For intricate shapes, discretization via unstructured grids makes direct potential calculation using quadrature prohibitively expensive. This study proposes a straightforward yet efficient high-order scheme for determining these potentials by employing Green's third identity to convert volume integrals into boundary forms that are well-suited for the Helsing-Ojala method. Consequently, the traditionally heavy computation time required for self-interaction and nearfield evaluations on unstructured grids becomes approximately equal to that of farfield interaction calculations on surfaces.
